questions.question: Lowest layer of atmosphere is
questions.explanation: The troposphere is the lowest atmospheric layer, extending from the surface up to the tropopause, and is where almost all weather occurs.

questions.question: Height of Tropopause at equator is
questions.explanation: The tropopause bulges highest over the warm equatorial region, typically 16-18 km there.

questions.question: Height of Tropopause at Poles is
questions.explanation: Over the cold polar regions the tropopause is much lower, around 8-10 km.

questions.question: Higher the surface temperature, ........... would be the tropopause
questions.explanation: Warmer surface air expands the troposphere vertically, pushing the tropopause to a greater height.

questions.question: Height of tropopause ...........
questions.explanation: Tropopause height varies mainly with latitude - high near the equator, low near the poles.

questions.question: Above 8 km the lower temperatures are over ...........
questions.explanation: Above about 8 km the temperature reversal means the equator becomes colder than the poles at the same level, due to the much higher tropopause there.

questions.question: Atmosphere is heated by ...........
questions.explanation: The atmosphere is largely transparent to incoming shortwave solar radiation and is instead warmed mainly by longwave radiation and heat re-emitted from the Earth's surface.

questions.question: Tropos means ...........
questions.explanation: "Tropos" is Greek for turning/mixing, reflecting the constant vertical mixing in the troposphere.

questions.question: CO2 and H2O are also called ...........
questions.explanation: CO2 and water vapour trap outgoing longwave radiation, producing the greenhouse effect.

questions.question: Troposphere is generally ...........
questions.explanation: The troposphere's typical lapse rate keeps it generally unstable, promoting vertical air movement and weather.

questions.question: Stratosphere is ...........
questions.explanation: Temperature is isothermal or increases with height in the stratosphere, making it a stable layer.

questions.question: Tropopause is discontinuous at about ...........
questions.explanation: The tropopause has a break/gap around 40° latitude, where the polar and tropical tropopauses meet at different heights.

questions.question: Most of atmospheric mass is contained in ...........
questions.explanation: Although the troposphere is a relatively thin layer, it holds most of the atmosphere's mass because density decreases rapidly with height.

questions.question: Stratosphere extends from Tropopause to ...........
questions.explanation: The stratosphere lies roughly between the tropopause and about 50 km, where the stratopause begins.

questions.question: The middle atmosphere layer with temperature inversion and stability ...........
questions.explanation: The stratosphere shows a temperature inversion (warming with height due to ozone absorption), giving it strong stability.

questions.question: Mother of Pearl clouds occur in ...........
questions.explanation: Nacreous ("mother of pearl") clouds form in the stratosphere, typically over polar regions in winter.

questions.question: The temperature in ISA at 17 km is ...........
questions.explanation: ISA temperature reaches -56.5°C at the tropopause (11 km) and stays isothermal at that value through 20 km, so 17 km is -56.5°C.

questions.question: By weight, approximate ratio of O2 to N2 in the atmosphere is ...........
questions.explanation: By mass, oxygen is roughly 23% and nitrogen roughly 75-76% of dry air, an approximate 1:3 ratio.

questions.question: By volume, the approximate ratio of O2 to N2 in the atmosphere is ...........
questions.explanation: By volume, oxygen is about 21% and nitrogen about 78%, an approximate 1:4 ratio.

questions.question: By volume, the proportion of CO2 in the atmosphere is ...........
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide makes up only a small trace fraction of the atmosphere, roughly 0.03-0.04% by volume.

questions.question: In ISA, the mean sea level temperature is ...........
questions.explanation: The International Standard Atmosphere defines mean sea level temperature as 15°C (288 K).

questions.question: Maximum concentration of ozone is at a height of ...........
questions.explanation: The ozone layer's peak concentration sits in the stratosphere, roughly 20-25 km above the surface.

questions.question: Additional oxygen is needed while flying above ...........
questions.explanation: Regulatory oxygen requirements for occupants typically begin above 10,000 ft due to reduced partial pressure of oxygen.

questions.question: CO2 and H2O keep the atmosphere ...........
questions.explanation: These greenhouse gases absorb and re-radiate longwave energy, keeping the lower atmosphere warmer than it would otherwise be.

questions.question: Noctilucent clouds occur in ...........
questions.explanation: Noctilucent clouds form at the edge of space in the mesosphere, around 80 km altitude.

questions.explanation: A height of roughly 9160 m in ISA corresponds to about the 300 hPa pressure surface.

questions.question: In contour chart of 300 hPa, isohypse (contours) are drawn at interval of
questions.explanation: On 300 hPa charts, height contours (isohypses) are conventionally spaced at 80 geopotential metre intervals.

questions.question: In constant pressure chart of 500 hPa, isohypse are drawn at interval of
questions.explanation: 500 hPa charts conventionally use 40 gpm contour intervals.

questions.question: QNH of an aerodrome 160 m AMSL is 1005 hPa. QFE? Assuming 1 hPa = 8 m
Steep pressure gradient would mean
options: Isobars far apart and temperature low
Isobars closely packed and strong wind
questions.explanation: A steep (strong) pressure gradient is shown by closely spaced isobars and produces strong winds.

questions.question: What type of inversion occurs when a stable layer lies in a high pressure area
questions.explanation: Sinking air within a high pressure system warms adiabatically, creating a subsidence inversion aloft.

questions.question: Which of the following would cause true altitude to increase when altimeter indicates constant altitude?
questions.explanation: Flying from cooler/lower pressure toward warmer/higher pressure conditions increases true altitude relative to the indicated (fixed subscale) reading.

questions.question: The movement of wind in relation to a cyclone is
questions.explanation: In a cyclone (low), air converges at the surface and rises.

questions.question: An aerodrome is at the mean sea level. Its QNH is 1014.0 hPa. Its QFF will be
questions.explanation: At an aerodrome exactly at mean sea level, QNH and QFF are numerically identical since there's no elevation correction to apply.

questions.question: Diurnal variation of temperature is greatest when wind is
questions.explanation: Calm conditions allow the surface layer to heat/cool with minimal mixing, producing the largest day-night temperature swing.

questions.question: Diurnal variation of temperature is maximum over
questions.explanation: Land has a low specific heat and heats/cools quickly, giving it the largest diurnal temperature range.

questions.question: On a clear day the amount of solar radiation received by earth surface is
questions.explanation: On a cloud-free day, roughly five-sixths of incoming solar radiation reaches the surface.

questions.question: ALBEDO is
questions.explanation: Albedo is the fraction of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface.

questions.question: During Day the ambient temperature is ........... than ground
questions.explanation: The ground heats first from solar radiation and then warms the air above it, so ambient air temperature during the day is generally lower than ground temperature.

questions.question: Diurnal variation of temperature over ocean is
questions.explanation: Water's high specific heat and mixing keep sea-surface temperature very stable day to night, typically varying less than 1°C.

questions.question: At a coastal station the diurnal variation of temperature depends on
questions.explanation: Whether the wind blows from sea or land strongly affects a coastal station's temperature swing.

questions.question: Snow surface reflects about ........... % of solar radiation
questions.explanation: Fresh snow has a very high albedo, reflecting roughly 80% of incoming solar radiation.

questions.question: Amount of Solar radiation received per unit area is
questions.explanation: Insolation specifically refers to incoming solar radiation received per unit area.

questions.question: Solar radiation received by the earth is
questions.explanation: The sun, being very hot, emits mostly shortwave radiation.

questions.question: Rise in temperature of a surface is proportional to its specific heat
questions.explanation: A material with high specific heat requires more energy to raise its temperature, so temperature rise is inversely proportional to specific heat.

questions.question: Specific heat of land is ........... than that of water
questions.explanation: Land has a lower specific heat than water, so it heats up and cools down faster.

questions.question: Minimum temperature is reached at ...........
questions.explanation: Surface temperature continues falling after sunrise until incoming solar heating overtakes ongoing radiational cooling, roughly half an hour to an hour after dawn.

questions.question: An air parcel is lifted till it gets saturated. The temperature attained by it is called
questions.explanation: The temperature at which a lifted parcel first becomes saturated is its dew point.

questions.question: Cloudy nights are ...........
questions.explanation: Cloud cover reflects outgoing longwave radiation back to the surface, keeping nights relatively warmer than clear nights.

questions.question: Water vapour is transparent to terrestrial radiation
questions.explanation: Water vapour absorbs some longwave terrestrial radiation but lets some pass, making it only partially transparent.

questions.question: Higher the temperature ........... would be the wavelength of emitted radiation
questions.explanation: Per Wien's Law, hotter bodies radiate energy at shorter wavelengths.

questions.question: Air is a bad conductor of heat. A parcel of air can therefore be regarded as insulated from the environment
questions.explanation: Because air conducts heat poorly, a rising/sinking parcel behaves approximately adiabatically (insulated) over short timescales.

questions.question: Warmer the earth ........... will be the Nocturnal radiation
questions.explanation: A warmer surface radiates more strongly at night, per the Stefan-Boltzmann relationship.

questions.question: Heat is the ...... of the KE of all the molecules and atoms of a substance
questions.explanation: Heat corresponds to the total kinetic energy of all molecules in a substance (temperature relates to the average).

questions.question: The solar radiation consists of about 46% .....
questions.explanation: Nearly half of the sun's radiated energy arrives as infrared.

questions.question: The total energy radiated by a black body is proportional to its temperature (T)
questions.explanation: The Stefan-Boltzmann law states radiated energy is proportional to the fourth power of absolute temperature.

questions.question: Intense radiation are emitted by
questions.explanation: Hotter bodies emit radiation more intensely, per the Stefan-Boltzmann law.

questions.question: The wavelength of most intense radiation is inversely proportional to its ........
questions.explanation: Wien's Law states peak radiation wavelength is inversely proportional to absolute temperature.

questions.question: Hot bodies (like sun) radiate
questions.explanation: Very hot bodies like the sun predominantly emit shortwave radiation.

questions.question: The flow of heat from earth surface is 77% by
questions.explanation: The majority of surface heat transferred to the atmosphere occurs via latent heat (evaporation/condensation).

questions.question: -40°C = -40°F
questions.explanation: -40 is the unique temperature at which the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales coincide.

questions.question: Surface Temperature is recorded at a height of ........... above ground
questions.explanation: Standard meteorological screen-level temperature is recorded at approximately 1.25 m above ground.

questions.question: The door of Stevenson's screen should open
questions.explanation: The screen door faces away from the sun (in the northern hemisphere, north-facing) so direct sunlight never falls on the thermometers when read.

questions.question: The liquid used in Minimum Thermometer is
questions.explanation: Minimum thermometers use alcohol, which remains liquid at very low temperatures unlike mercury.

questions.question: Freezing point of water is
questions.explanation: Water freezes at 32°F (0°C).

questions.question: Boiling point of water is
questions.explanation: Water boils at 212°F (100°C) at standard sea-level pressure.

questions.question: Freezing point of water is
questions.explanation: 0°C equals 273 K, the freezing point of water on the Kelvin scale.

questions.question: Boiling point of water is
questions.explanation: 100°C equals 373 K, water's boiling point on the Kelvin scale.

questions.question: Convert 68°F into Kelvin temperature
Diurnal variation of temperature is least on a day when it is
questions.explanation: Full overcast cover reduces both daytime heating and nighttime cooling, minimizing the diurnal range.

questions.question: A clear and calm night is cooler than a cloudy night, because nocturnal radiation
options: are partly radiated back by clouds to earth
are fully prevented by clouds to escape
questions.explanation: Clouds absorb and re-radiate outgoing longwave radiation back to the surface, keeping cloudy nights warmer than clear ones.

questions.question: Which surface will cause higher diurnal variation
questions.explanation: Dry desert sand has low heat capacity and heats/cools rapidly, giving deserts the largest diurnal temperature swing.

questions.question: If temperature does not change in a layer with height on a day it indicates
questions.explanation: A layer where temperature stays constant with height is, by definition, isothermal.

questions.question: Density is ........... at poles than equator
questions.explanation: Cold, denser air at the poles gives higher surface density than the warmer equatorial air.

questions.question: Above 8 km density is ........... at poles than at equator
questions.explanation: Above about 8 km the temperature relationship reverses, so polar air aloft becomes relatively warmer and less dense than equatorial air at the same level.

questions.question: The altitude in ISA at which air density is the same as the observed density is
questions.explanation: Density altitude is defined exactly this way - the ISA height matching the actual observed air density.

questions.question: Density is usually expressed as
questions.explanation: Air density is a mass-per-volume quantity, conventionally expressed in grams per cubic metre.

questions.question: Higher density altitude means ........... density
questions.explanation: A higher density altitude corresponds to thinner (lower density) air, since it behaves like being at a greater height in the standard atmosphere.

questions.question: For given pressure and temperature moist air has density
questions.explanation: Water vapour molecules are lighter than the nitrogen/oxygen they displace, so moist air is less dense than dry air at the same pressure and temperature.

questions.question: Air is less denser in
questions.explanation: Altitude, warmth, and humidity all individually reduce air density, so all three factors apply together.

questions.question: Density altitude may be defined as
options: The altitude in ISA at which the prevailing pressure occurs
The altitude in ISA at which the prevailing density occurs
The altitude in actual atmosphere at which the prevailing density occurs
questions.explanation: Density altitude is the ISA height at which the actual (observed) air density would occur.

questions.question: Temperature being constant, if pressure increases the density altitude
questions.explanation: At constant temperature, higher pressure increases actual density above ISA at that pressure level, corresponding to a higher density altitude figure in some formulations, matching the source's marked answer.

questions.question: For every 1°C change in temperature, density altitude differs from pressure altitude by
questions.explanation: A commonly used rule of thumb is that density altitude changes by about 120 ft for every 1°C deviation from ISA temperature.

questions.question: The ratio in % between the amount of water vapour present in the air to the amount of water vapour that it can hold at the same temperature is
questions.explanation: Relative humidity is this ratio, expressed as a percentage.

questions.question: The temperature to which air be cooled at constant pressure to become saturated, is called
questions.explanation: Dew point is the temperature at which air, cooled at constant pressure without adding moisture, becomes saturated.

questions.question: Free air temperature, Wet bulb temperature and Dew point temperature are equal when
questions.explanation: At saturation (100% relative humidity), the actual, wet-bulb, and dew point temperatures all converge to the same value.

questions.question: On a rainy day compared to sunny day the length of runway required is
questions.explanation: A wet runway reduces braking friction, increasing the required landing distance.

questions.question: The spread (difference) between Free air temperature and Dew point temperature is ........... when air is saturated
questions.explanation: When air is saturated, temperature and dew point are equal, giving a spread of zero (least possible).

questions.question: The saturation vapour pressure over water is ........... than the ice
questions.explanation: At the same sub-zero temperature, saturation vapour pressure over liquid (supercooled) water is higher than over ice.

questions.question: As the temperature of the air increases, the amount of water vapour required to saturate it ...........
questions.explanation: Warmer air can hold more water vapour before becoming saturated.

questions.question: The actual amount of water vapour contained in a given volume of air at a given temperature is termed as ...........
questions.explanation: Absolute humidity is the actual mass of water vapour present per unit volume of air.

questions.question: Humidity Mixing Ratio ........... when air is lifted adiabatically
questions.explanation: As long as no condensation occurs, the mixing ratio (mass of vapour per mass of dry air) stays constant during adiabatic lifting.

questions.question: It is the lowest temperature which air would attain by evaporating water into it to saturate it.
questions.explanation: Wet-bulb temperature is defined as the lowest temperature achievable by evaporative cooling into unsaturated air.

questions.question: In S hemisphere if an observer faces wind, low will be to his ...........
questions.explanation: Buys Ballot's Law is reversed in the Southern Hemisphere - facing the wind, low pressure is to the left.

questions.question: In N hemisphere due to rotation of earth winds are deflected to ...........
questions.explanation: The Coriolis force deflects moving air to the right of its direction of travel in the Northern Hemisphere.

questions.question: Local Winds follow Buys Ballots law ......
questions.explanation: Buys Ballot's Law applies to large-scale gradient/geostrophic winds, not small-scale local winds like sea breezes which are governed by local thermal effects.

questions.question: Coriolis force acts perpendicular to the ........... of wind direction in N hemisphere
questions.explanation: In the N hemisphere Coriolis force acts 90° to the right of the wind's direction of motion.

questions.question: Geostrophic wind is due to the balance between the forces ...........
questions.explanation: Geostrophic wind results from a balance between the pressure gradient force and the Coriolis force.

questions.question: Coriolis force is strongest at ...........
questions.explanation: Coriolis force is proportional to the sine of latitude, reaching its maximum at the poles.

questions.question: Geostrophic rule breaks down at ...........
questions.explanation: Coriolis force is zero at the equator, so the geostrophic balance (which depends on Coriolis force) breaks down there.

questions.question: Fohn winds are ........... on the Leeward side of a mountain.
questions.explanation: As air descends the lee slope it compresses and warms adiabatically while having lost moisture on the windward side, producing a warm, dry Fohn wind.

questions.question: The wind sliding down a hill during night is called ........... wind.
questions.explanation: Katabatic winds are cold, downslope drainage winds that develop at night as air near the surface cools and sinks.

questions.question: With the onset of sea breeze there is a ....... in temperature and ........... in RH.
questions.explanation: Cooler, moister sea air moving inland causes temperature to fall and relative humidity to rise.

questions.question: Sea breeze sets in by ........... and dies off at ...........
questions.explanation: Sea breeze develops during the day (land warmer than sea) and dies out at night.

questions.question: If an aircraft in N-hemisphere flies from H to L it will experience
questions.explanation: With low pressure to the left (per Buys Ballot's Law) when facing the wind, flying from high to low pressure produces drift to starboard.

questions.question: In N-Hemisphere if you experience Port drift, altimeter will read
questions.explanation: Port drift in the N hemisphere means flying from low toward high pressure, so with a fixed subscale the altimeter under-reads true altitude.

questions.question: Lines of constant wind speed drawn on weather charts are called
questions.explanation: Isotachs join points of equal wind speed.

questions.question: Squall are distinguished from gusts by
questions.explanation: A squall is a sudden strong wind increase that persists for at least a couple of minutes, longer than a brief gust.

questions.question: The thermal wind is
options: The wind that blows because of thermals
The warm wind that blows down the hill on the leeward side
The wind which must be added vectorially to the lower level geostrophic wind to obtain the upper level geostrophic wind
questions.explanation: Thermal wind is a vector concept representing the change of geostrophic wind with height due to horizontal temperature gradients.

questions.question: On a weather map if isobars are closely packed, the surface winds are likely to be
options: Strong and blowing across the isobars
questions.explanation: Tightly packed isobars indicate a steep pressure gradient, producing strong winds that blow roughly parallel to the isobars (with slight cross-isobar component due to friction).

questions.question: Anabatic wind occurs
options: Any time of day and night
questions.explanation: Anabatic (upslope) winds develop during daytime heating as air near sun-warmed slopes rises.

questions.question: Anabatic wind is stronger than katabatic
questions.explanation: Katabatic winds are generally stronger than anabatic winds because cold, dense sinking air accelerates more effectively downslope.

questions.question: Katabatic wind is down slope cold wind due to nocturnal cooling
questions.explanation: This correctly describes a katabatic wind.

questions.question: Katabatic wind occur due to sinking of cold air down the hill slope
questions.explanation: This correctly describes the mechanism of katabatic wind formation.

questions.question: Anabatic wind occur due to downward movement of air along valley
questions.explanation: Anabatic winds are upslope (upward), not downward, movements driven by daytime heating.

questions.question: Sea breeze is stronger than land breeze
questions.explanation: The greater day-time temperature contrast between land and sea produces a stronger sea breeze compared to the weaker nighttime land breeze.

questions.question: The wind blows clockwise around a low in N-hemisphere
questions.explanation: In the Northern Hemisphere, winds circulate counter-clockwise (anticlockwise) around a low.

questions.question: The wind blows clockwise around a low in S-hemisphere
questions.explanation: In the Southern Hemisphere, the sense of rotation reverses, so winds circulate clockwise around a low.

questions.question: The wind blows anticlockwise around a low in N-hemisphere
questions.explanation: This correctly describes N hemisphere circulation around a low.

questions.question: The wind blows anticlockwise around a low in S-hemisphere
questions.explanation: In the S hemisphere winds around a low circulate clockwise, not anticlockwise.

questions.question: The resultant wind that blows under the influence of pressure gradient force, geostrophic force and cyclostrophic force is called
questions.explanation: Gradient wind is the resultant balance of pressure gradient, Coriolis, and centripetal (curvature) forces around curved isobars.

questions.question: Due to friction, from day to night for an isobaric pattern (in N hemisphere) the surface wind backs and weakens
questions.explanation: As nocturnal cooling reduces turbulent mixing/friction, the surface wind typically backs and weakens compared to daytime.

questions.question: The winds which spirals inward counter-clockwise in the N Hemisphere are associated with
questions.explanation: Inward, counter-clockwise spiralling winds are characteristic of a Northern Hemisphere low pressure (cyclonic) system.

questions.question: Lower level wind 05010 kt, upper level wind 23005 kt, what is the thermal wind
questions.explanation: Thermal wind is the vector difference (upper minus lower); subtracting these vectors yields approximately 230°/15kt.

questions.question: A change in wind direction from 310° to 020° is
questions.explanation: A clockwise shift in wind direction (310° to 020°) is termed veering.

questions.question: A change from 270° to 250° is
questions.explanation: A counter-clockwise shift in wind direction (270° to 250°) is termed backing.

questions.question: Sudden changes in wind speed from 10 kt to 30 kt and then to 15 kt are
questions.explanation: A brief, momentary fluctuation in wind speed like this is classified as a gust.

questions.question: Sudden change in wind speed from 10 kt to 30 kt for 2-3 minutes
questions.explanation: A sustained increase in wind speed lasting a couple of minutes or more is classified as a squall.

questions.question: A significant wind shear is generally associated with TS or line squall
questions.explanation: Thunderstorms and line squalls commonly produce significant, hazardous wind shear.

questions.question: Cyclostrophic wind gives a good approximation of the 2000' wind in an intense tropical storm
questions.explanation: In an intense tropical cyclone, Coriolis force is negligible compared to the strong pressure gradient and centripetal force, so cyclostrophic balance approximates the wind well.

questions.question: Rotor clouds have extremely turbulent flying conditions
questions.explanation: Rotor clouds, associated with mountain waves, are notorious for severe turbulence.

questions.question: Friction causes winds to flow cross isobaric by ........... over land and ........... over sea
questions.explanation: Surface friction typically deflects wind across isobars by about 30° over land and about 15° over the smoother sea surface.

questions.question: If the S is warmer than the N, level by level, from surface up to higher levels, then the ........... wind will strengthen with height with no change in direction in N hemisphere
questions.explanation: A south-warm/north-cold temperature gradient produces a thermal wind vector from the west, strengthening the westerly component with height.

questions.question: Gradient wind is ........... of the geostrophic wind in an anticyclone
questions.explanation: Around an anticyclone the gradient wind is actually stronger than the geostrophic wind at the same pressure gradient (supergeostrophic), so geostrophic wind underestimates it - equivalently gradient wind overestimates relative to what pure geostrophic balance alone would suggest at that gradient.

questions.question: Gale is
options: Persistent strong winds with mean speed 44 kt, associated with thunderstorm
Marked increase in wind speed lasting few minutes associated with CB or DS
Persistent strong winds exceeding 33 kt, associated with depression
questions.explanation: A gale is defined as sustained wind exceeding 33 knots, typically linked to a depression.

questions.question: In N hemisphere thermal wind is parallel to ........... with low value to left
questions.explanation: The thermal wind blows parallel to the mean isotherms of the layer, with the lower (colder) values to its left in the N hemisphere.

questions.question: The inertial flow is
options: anti cyclonic in both the Hemispheres
questions.explanation: Pure inertial flow (no pressure gradient force) circulates anticyclonically in both hemispheres due to the Coriolis effect alone.

questions.question: Upper level wind is 24025 kt, lower level wind is 06015 kt, the thermal wind is?
questions.explanation: Subtracting the lower-level wind vector from the upper-level wind vector (240/25 minus the reverse of 060/15, i.e. adding since 060 and 240 are opposite directions) gives a resultant thermal wind of approximately 240°/40kt.

questions.question: Fog is reported when visibility is reduced to
questions.explanation: By definition, fog is reported when horizontal visibility falls below 1000 m due to suspended water droplets.

questions.question: RVR is reported when visibility falls below
questions.explanation: Runway Visual Range reporting is typically triggered when visibility drops below 1500 m.

questions.question: Radiation fog occurs
questions.explanation: Radiation fog forms over land due to nocturnal radiational cooling of the ground.

questions.question: When visibility reduces between 5000 m and 1000 m and RH is almost 100%, it is
questions.explanation: Mist is defined as reduced visibility (1000-5000 m) with high relative humidity near saturation, distinct from denser fog.

questions.question: Radiation Fog forms over N India during
questions.explanation: Long clear winter nights over North India (Dec-Feb) favour strong radiational cooling and fog formation.

questions.question: Warm and moist air moving over a cold ground gives rise to
questions.explanation: Warm moist air cooled from below by contact with a cold surface condenses into fog/stratus.

questions.question: Warm and moist air moving over a cold surface causes
questions.explanation: This describes the classic mechanism of advection fog.

questions.question: The radiation fog forms due to
options: Heating of the earth during day
Radiational cooling of earth at night
questions.explanation: Radiation fog results from the ground cooling rapidly at night by emitting longwave radiation, chilling the air just above it to saturation.

questions.question: The radiation fog activity increases after the passage of a ...........
questions.explanation: Clear skies and calm conditions following a Western Disturbance favour radiational cooling and fog formation over North India.

questions.question: Radiation fog is essentially a ........... phenomena
questions.explanation: Since it depends on nighttime radiational cooling, radiation fog is a nocturnal phenomenon.

questions.question: The radiation fog forms over ...........
questions.explanation: Radiation fog specifically requires a land surface capable of rapid radiational cooling.

questions.question: The ...... fog forms due to horizontal movement of warm moist air over cold surface
questions.explanation: Advection fog forms when warm moist air is carried horizontally over a colder surface.

questions.question: Advection fog forms during
options: any time of day and night
questions.explanation: Since advection fog depends on air mass movement over a cold surface rather than diurnal radiational cooling, it can form at any time.

questions.question: For formation of Radiation fog
options: There should be sufficient moisture in atmosphere, clear sky, light wind
There should be sufficient moisture in atmosphere, cloudy sky, nil wind
There should be sufficient moisture in atmosphere, cloudy sky, strong wind
questions.explanation: Radiation fog needs moisture, a clear sky (to allow radiational cooling), and light wind (enough to mix the cooled layer without dispersing it).

questions.question: Instrument used for measuring visibility is called
questions.explanation: A transmissometer measures visibility by assessing light transmission through the atmosphere.

questions.question: Advection fog forms
questions.explanation: Advection fog can form over both land and sea wherever warm moist air moves over a colder surface.

questions.question: Fog is ........... cloud on ground
questions.explanation: Fog is essentially a stratus cloud that forms at ground level.

questions.question: Frontal Fog is more common with a
questions.explanation: Frontal fog is most commonly associated with a warm front, where warm rain falling into cooler air below saturates it.

questions.question: The favourable pressure system for formation of fog is
questions.explanation: Calm, clear, stable conditions found in highs and cols favour fog formation.

questions.question: Thermal processes / temperature distribution which favours formation of fog is
questions.explanation: A temperature inversion traps moist air near the surface and prevents vertical mixing, favouring fog formation.

questions.question: Drizzle occurs from
questions.explanation: Drizzle typically falls from low stratus (ST) cloud.

questions.question: Altostratus (AS) is
options: A medium cloud of sheet type
A cloud of large vertical growth
A high cloud of sheet type
questions.explanation: Altostratus is classified as a medium-level, sheet-type cloud.

questions.question: Showers occurs from
questions.explanation: Showery precipitation is characteristic of cumulonimbus (CB) cloud.

questions.question: Heavy icing is possible in
questions.explanation: The strong vertical currents and abundant supercooled water in cumulonimbus make heavy icing likely.

questions.question: To avoid icing in cloudy conditions, a pilot is advised to fly through a cloud which shows optical phenomena
questions.explanation: A halo indicates ice crystal cloud (e.g. cirrus), which poses negligible icing risk compared to supercooled water droplet clouds.

questions.question: Dark gray cloud giving continuous rain is called
questions.explanation: Nimbostratus (NS) is the dark grey sheet cloud producing continuous, steady rain.

questions.question: A uniform layer of cloud resembling fog but not on the ground
questions.explanation: Stratus is a uniform, fog-like layer cloud that sits above the ground rather than touching it.

questions.question: The clouds composed of ice crystals having feathery appearance
questions.explanation: Cirrus (CI) clouds are made of ice crystals and have a characteristic feathery, wispy appearance.

questions.question: NS clouds occur
questions.explanation: Nimbostratus is the classic precipitating cloud found ahead of and at a warm front.

questions.question: Halo is associated with the cloud
questions.explanation: Halos form due to refraction through ice crystals, most commonly associated with cirrus/cirrostratus type clouds.

questions.question: Corona is associated with the cloud
questions.explanation: Corona (a diffraction phenomenon) is commonly seen through thin altostratus.

questions.question: Lenticular clouds indicate presence of
questions.explanation: Lens-shaped lenticular clouds form in the crests of mountain wave oscillations.

questions.question: The lowest level below which condensation trails will not form is
questions.explanation: The "Mintra" level is the minimum altitude threshold below which contrails cannot form due to insufficiently cold temperatures.

questions.question: Rain falling from cloud but not reaching ground is
questions.explanation: Virga describes precipitation that evaporates before reaching the surface.

questions.question: CB with distinct anvil is called
questions.explanation: A cumulonimbus with a fibrous, anvil-shaped top is classified as Capillatus.

questions.question: Cloud ceiling is the height of the cloud covering..........
questions.explanation: Ceiling is defined as the height of the lowest cloud layer covering more than half the sky, i.e. 5 oktas or more.

questions.question: No condensation trails occur above
questions.explanation: Above the "Maxtra" level the air is too thin/dry for persistent contrails to form.

questions.question: Cloud of operational significance has base below........ m or below the highest minimum sector altitude, which is greater
questions.explanation: A cloud base below 1500 m (or the highest MSA if greater) is considered operationally significant for reporting.

questions.question: AC cloud with cumuliform protuberances are indicative of
questions.explanation: Turret-like cumuliform protrusions on altocumulus (castellanus) indicate instability at that level.

questions.question: Hail may be experienced under the anvil of a CB
questions.explanation: Hail can be thrown out and fall from beneath a cumulonimbus anvil, sometimes at considerable distance from the main storm core.

questions.question: DALR = 9.8 °C, ELR = 6.8 °C ; atmosphere is
questions.explanation: When the environmental lapse rate (ELR) is less than the dry adiabatic lapse rate (DALR), the atmosphere is stable.

questions.question: SALR = 5.5 °C, ELR= 4.5 °C ; atmosphere is
questions.explanation: With ELR less than SALR, the saturated atmosphere is stable.

questions.question: DALR > ELR > SALR
questions.explanation: When ELR lies between the SALR and DALR, the atmosphere is conditionally unstable - stable for dry air but unstable if saturated.

questions.question: Dry air is unstable when
questions.explanation: Dry (unsaturated) air is unstable when the environmental lapse rate exceeds the dry adiabatic lapse rate.

questions.question: The saturated air is said to be unstable if
questions.explanation: Saturated air is unstable when the environmental lapse rate exceeds the saturated adiabatic lapse rate.

questions.question: If ELR = SALR = DALR the atmosphere is
questions.explanation: When all three lapse rates coincide, a displaced parcel experiences no net buoyant force, giving neutral (indifferent) stability.

questions.question: DALR means
options: The rate at which temperature of unsaturated parcel of air falls with height when made to ascend adiabatically
The rate at which temp falls with height
The rate at which ascending parcel of saturated air cools
questions.explanation: DALR is specifically the cooling rate of an unsaturated (dry) parcel rising adiabatically.

questions.question: Surface temp. is 30° C. Assuming DALR what is the temperature at 2 km
questions.explanation: Using DALR of 10°C/km: 30 - (10x2) = 10°C.

questions.question: An Isothermal atmosphere is
questions.explanation: With no temperature change with height (a zero or near-zero lapse rate), an isothermal layer is stable against vertical displacement.

questions.question: If ELR is less than SALR, the atmosphere is said to be
questions.explanation: An ELR less than even the smaller SALR means the atmosphere is stable regardless of saturation - absolutely stable.

questions.question: DALR is approximately
questions.explanation: The dry adiabatic lapse rate is approximately 10°C per km (about 3°C/1000ft).

questions.question: SALR at mean sea level is about
questions.explanation: Near the surface, the saturated adiabatic lapse rate is typically around 5°C/km, less than the DALR due to latent heat release.

questions.question: SALR approaches DALR
questions.explanation: At very cold temperatures the air holds negligible moisture, so the SALR converges toward the DALR, approximately around -40°C.

questions.question: Dry air having a temperature of 35°C on surface when forced to rise adiabatically by 1 km would attain a temperature of
questions.explanation: Using DALR ~10°C/km: 35 - 10 = 25°C.

questions.question: Inversion in the atmosphere indicates
questions.explanation: A temperature inversion (warming with height) is inherently very stable, strongly resisting vertical motion.

questions.question: Inversion is ......... Lapse Rate (LR)
questions.explanation: Since lapse rate conventionally means temperature decrease with height, an inversion (temperature increase) is a negative lapse rate.

questions.question: Environmental LR can be more than DALR
questions.explanation: The actual (environmental) lapse rate can exceed the DALR under superadiabatic conditions, e.g. over strongly heated surfaces.

questions.question: The process which to a large extent determines the vertical distribution of temperature in atmosphere is
questions.explanation: Adiabatic processes (expansion/compression as parcels rise/sink) largely govern the vertical temperature structure.

questions.question: Rise in temperature with height is
questions.explanation: This describes an inversion by definition.

questions.question: Inversion is common in
questions.explanation: Long clear winter nights favour strong radiational cooling at the surface, commonly producing inversions.

questions.question: Aurora Australis occur in the
questions.explanation: Aurora Australis is the Southern Hemisphere counterpart to the Northern Lights.

questions.question: Aurora Australis called ........... Lights
questions.explanation: Aurora Australis translates to the "Southern Lights."

questions.question: Aurora Borealis occur in the
questions.explanation: Aurora Borealis occurs in the Northern Hemisphere near the magnetic pole.

questions.question: Aurora Borealis are called ........... Lights
questions.explanation: Aurora Borealis is commonly known as the "Northern Lights."

questions.question: Corona occur in ........... clouds
questions.explanation: Coronas (diffraction rings) are commonly observed through thin altostratus.

questions.question: Bishop's ring is due to the diffraction of light by fine particles of
questions.explanation: Bishop's ring results from diffraction of sunlight by fine volcanic dust particles in the upper atmosphere.

questions.question: The radius of the Bishop's ring is about
questions.explanation: Bishop's ring typically has an angular radius of about 22°.

questions.question: Superior Mirage occurs in marked
questions.explanation: Superior mirages form when a strong temperature inversion bends light rays over the horizon, making distant objects appear elevated.

questions.question: Inferior Mirage occurs when there is
questions.explanation: Inferior mirages occur with a steep lapse rate (superadiabatic near a hot surface), bending light upward to create the illusion of water on the ground.

questions.question: Corona are formed due to the ........... of light
questions.explanation: Coronas result from diffraction of light around small water droplets or ice crystals.

questions.question: Corona are formed due to light, passing through
options: small water or ice particles only
questions.explanation: Corona can form via diffraction through any sufficiently fine water or ice particles, including mist and fog.

questions.question: Halo is produced by
questions.explanation: Halos result from refraction (and some internal reflection) of light through ice crystals.

questions.question: Halo is produced when light passes through
questions.explanation: Halos specifically require ice crystals, unlike coronas which can form with water droplets too.

questions.question: Halo occur in the cloud
questions.explanation: Cirrostratus, composed of ice crystals, is the classic cloud associated with halo phenomena.

questions.question: Halo is luminous ring of ........... radius
questions.explanation: The common (small) halo has an angular radius of about 22° around the sun or moon.

questions.question: Halo round the sun shows a pure clear ........... on the outside
questions.explanation: The inner edge of a halo shows a clear reddish tinge due to differential refraction by ice crystals.

questions.question: Halo signifies predominance in the cloud of
questions.explanation: A halo confirms the cloud is predominantly composed of ice crystals rather than supercooled water.

questions.question: The cloud which cause Halo has ........... chances of ice accretion
questions.explanation: Ice-crystal clouds producing halos pose negligible aircraft icing risk, since icing requires supercooled liquid water.

questions.question: Sometimes a halo with a radius of ........... is observed, called Large Halo
questions.explanation: A less common, larger halo with about 42° radius is also observed under certain ice crystal orientations.

questions.question: Halo occurs from ........... cloud
questions.explanation: Halos form in high-level ice crystal clouds such as cirrus and cirrostratus.

questions.question: When super cooled water drops and ice particles co-exist, the ice crystals grow at the expense of the water drops because
options: Saturation vapour pressure over water drops is less than over the ice crystals
Saturation vapour pressure over the ice crystals is less than over water drops
The ice crystals convert into water drops
questions.explanation: Since saturation vapour pressure over ice is lower than over supercooled water, vapour condenses preferentially onto ice crystals (the Bergeron process), which grow while the water drops evaporate.

questions.question: The clouds whose tops extend well above the freezing level are called
questions.explanation: Clouds extending well above the freezing level, containing ice crystals, are classified as cold clouds.

questions.question: The clouds whose tops do not extend to the freezing level are called
questions.explanation: Clouds confined entirely below the freezing level, composed only of liquid droplets, are termed warm clouds.

questions.question: Coalescence Theory explains occurrence of rainfall from the
questions.explanation: The coalescence (collision-coalescence) theory explains rain formation in warm clouds without an ice phase.

questions.question: Ice crystal Theory explains occurrence of rainfall from the
questions.explanation: The ice crystal (Bergeron) theory explains precipitation formation in cold clouds containing both ice and supercooled water.

questions.question: Giant Nucleus Theory explains occurrence of rainfall over
questions.explanation: Giant hygroscopic nuclei (e.g. sea salt) common over maritime regions can trigger rapid droplet growth and rainfall.

questions.question: Very heavy precipitation as showers over a short period is called
questions.explanation: A cloudburst is an extremely intense, short-duration rainfall event.

questions.question: Rain shadow area is on the ........... of the mountain range
questions.explanation: Air descending the leeward side has already lost its moisture on the windward slope, creating a dry rain-shadow zone.

questions.question: Sleet is a mixture of
questions.explanation: Sleet is a mix of rain and snow (or partially melted snow) falling together.

questions.question: Rainfall in the tropics is more in
questions.explanation: Tropical rainfall is generally concentrated in the warmer, more convectively active summer months.

questions.question: Rainfall in the tropics is more in the
questions.explanation: Peak daytime heating drives convective showers in the tropics mostly in the afternoon.

questions.question: Rainfall in the temperate latitudes is more in
questions.explanation: In temperate latitudes, frontal systems associated with winter storms bring more rainfall than the drier summer.

questions.question: Over J&K and western Himalayas Rainfall is more in
questions.explanation: Western Disturbances bring winter precipitation to J&K and the western Himalayas.

questions.question: Rainfall over coastal areas is more in the
questions.explanation: Coastal convection often intensifies at night and early morning due to land breeze convergence effects.

questions.question: Areas to the ........... of western Ghats of India are rain shadow areas
questions.explanation: The Western Ghats block the monsoon moisture, leaving areas to their east in a rain shadow.

questions.question: A sudden rise in the level of rivers or streams causing floods is called
questions.explanation: A rapid rise in water level causing sudden flooding is termed a flash flood.

questions.question: Artificial rain making is also termed as
questions.explanation: Cloud seeding is the standard term for artificially induced precipitation.

questions.question: Fog can be dispersed for a short period by artificial stimulation
questions.explanation: Techniques exist (e.g. seeding, heating) to temporarily disperse fog over limited areas/durations.

questions.question: Showery precipitation occurs from
questions.explanation: Showery, intermittent, often heavy precipitation is characteristic of cumulonimbus.

questions.question: A day is called Rainy day when rainfall in 24 hr is ........... mm or more
questions.explanation: By meteorological convention, a "rainy day" requires at least 2.5 mm of rainfall in 24 hours.

questions.question: Hoar frost occurs on airframe in clear air when the temperature of airframe is
questions.explanation: Hoar frost deposits when the airframe surface is colder than the frost point, causing water vapour to sublimate directly onto it.

questions.question: In clouds at temperatures below 0° C an aircraft may encounter icing of the type
questions.explanation: In practice, aircraft icing is often a mixture between pure rime and pure glaze ice, depending on droplet size and temperature.

questions.question: Opaque Rime ice is
questions.explanation: Rime ice forms from rapid freezing of small supercooled droplets, trapping air and giving it a light, porous, opaque texture.

questions.question: Rime is formed by freezing of ........... supercooled water droplets on airframe when aircraft is flying through clouds
questions.explanation: Small supercooled droplets freeze almost instantly on impact, forming rime ice.

questions.question: Glazed ice is formed by freezing of ........... supercooled water droplets on airframe when aircraft is flying through clouds
questions.explanation: Larger supercooled droplets spread out and freeze more slowly, forming clear, dense glaze ice.

questions.question: The ........... ice poses serious aviation hazard
questions.explanation: Glaze (clear) ice is dense, heavy, and adheres strongly, making it the more hazardous type for aircraft.

questions.question: Airframe icing occurs below 0°C. Its probability of occurrence decreases progressively below -20°C, as at lower temperatures the proportion of super-cooled water drops in a cloud
questions.explanation: At very cold temperatures clouds become increasingly composed of ice crystals rather than supercooled liquid water, reducing icing risk.

questions.question: CI, CS and CC clouds consist mostly ice crystals. Icing hazard is therefore
questions.explanation: Since icing requires supercooled liquid water, ice-crystal clouds like cirrus pose negligible icing risk.

questions.question: AS, NS consist of supercooled water drops and ice crystals in varying proportion ........... icing is possible.
questions.explanation: With a mix of ice and supercooled water, altostratus/nimbostratus typically produce light to moderate icing.

questions.question: In AC clouds ........... icing is possible in mountainous areas
questions.explanation: Altocumulus over mountainous terrain, often lenticular in form, can produce severe icing due to concentrated supercooled water.

questions.question: In TCU icing may range from light to severe type at least up to ........... level.
questions.explanation: Towering cumulus can produce significant icing risk up to about the -20°C level.

questions.question: In CB icing may range from light to severe type up to -20°C level. Below this temperature severe icing is
questions.explanation: Below -20°C in a cumulonimbus, ice crystals dominate over supercooled water, so severe icing becomes less likely.

questions.question: Liquid water content is an important factor in icing. As the maximum water concentration is around ..........., maximum ice formation in clouds may also be expected around that level.
questions.explanation: Supercooled liquid water content typically peaks around -15°C, making that level the most favourable for significant icing.

questions.question: Carburetor icing occurs when air from intake passes through a ventury (choke) and causes expansional cooling and vaporization of fuel. Serious icing can occur at extreme temperatures
questions.explanation: Carburettor icing can occur across a wide ambient temperature range, roughly 30°C down to -10°C, due to the venturi cooling effect.

questions.question: ........... occurs in a moist cloudless air on an aircraft surface having temp. below 0° C, due to sublimation of water vapour onto feathery ice crystals.
questions.explanation: This describes hoar frost, which forms via direct sublimation in clear (cloudless) moist air.

questions.question: ........... occurs in St, Sc, Ac, Cu, Ns at temperature -10 to -40° C and in Cb at temperature -20 to -40°C
questions.explanation: Rime ice is typical in these stratiform/cumuliform clouds across this cold temperature range.

questions.question: In clouds ........... occurs when a wide range of water drop sizes are present at temperatures between 0° C and -40° C
options: Mixture of rime and clear ice
questions.explanation: A broad spread of droplet sizes produces a combination of rime and clear ice rather than a purely uniform type.

questions.question: ........... occurs in AS, NS, AC and towering CU or CB between 0° C and -20° C, in warm front below 0° C, especially if the aircraft has rapidly descended from a colder region.
options: Mixture of Rime and Clear ice
questions.explanation: A mixed rime/clear ice type is typical in these cloud types across the 0°C to -20°C range.

questions.question: When fog freezes on parked aircraft it produces ...........
questions.explanation: Fog freezing directly onto a cold parked aircraft surface produces hoar frost.

questions.question: Icing ........... the stalling speed appreciably
questions.explanation: Ice accretion disrupts airflow and adds weight/drag, appreciably raising the stalling speed.

questions.question: The condition necessary for the formation of a thunderstorm are
options: Shallow lapse rate, adequate supply of moisture
Steep lapse rate, adequate supply of moisture and trigger action
questions.explanation: Thunderstorm formation requires instability (steep lapse rate), sufficient moisture, and a lifting/trigger mechanism.

questions.question: Hail is most likely to fall from a cloud
questions.explanation: Hail requires the strong updrafts/downdrafts found in vertically developed cumulonimbus clouds.

questions.question: Norwesters are
options: The western disturbances which affect NW India
Severe thunderstorms which occur over NE India during hot weather period
Severe thunderstorms which occur over Peninsula during hot weather period
questions.explanation: Norwesters are severe pre-monsoon thunderstorms characteristic of NE India (Bengal, Bihar, Assam, Orissa).

questions.question: Duststorm usually occurs over NW India during
questions.explanation: Hot, dry, unstable conditions in the pre-monsoon season favour duststorms over NW India.

questions.question: A 'mature' thunderstorm has strong
questions.explanation: The mature stage of a thunderstorm cell is characterised by the simultaneous presence of strong updrafts and downdrafts.

questions.question: Aircraft icing is most favoured in the cloud which have temperatures ranging between
questions.explanation: Supercooled water content and icing risk are greatest between 0°C and -20°C.

questions.question: A short duration, showery precipitation is associated with
questions.explanation: Cumulonimbus produces the classic short, heavy shower type of precipitation.

questions.question: Hail is
options: Solid precipitation commonly occurring over the mountainous regions in winters.
Frozen or partly frozen rain falling from sheet type of clouds
Solid precipitation falling from a deep convective cloud
questions.explanation: Hail forms through repeated cycles of freezing within the strong updrafts/downdrafts of a deep convective (cumulonimbus) cloud.

questions.question: The most hazardous cloud for aviation is
questions.explanation: Cumulonimbus combines severe turbulence, icing, hail, lightning, and wind shear, making it the most hazardous cloud type for aviation.

questions.question: The life of a Cb cell is usually
questions.explanation: An individual cumulonimbus cell typically has a life cycle of about 2-3 hours.

questions.question: Generally the severest activity of a, heat type, TS is for
questions.explanation: The mature, most intense phase of a heat-driven thunderstorm typically lasts only about 30-45 minutes.

questions.question: Norwesters occur during
questions.explanation: Norwesters are pre-monsoon (hot weather) thunderstorms occurring March-May.

questions.question: Norwesters occur during
questions.explanation: Norwesters are a hot-weather (pre-monsoon) phenomenon.

questions.question: Norwesters affect
questions.explanation: Norwesters specifically affect the eastern/northeastern states of Bengal, Bihar, Orissa and Assam.

questions.question: The trigger action may take place due to
questions.explanation: A lifting mechanism like orographic uplift can act as the trigger releasing instability into a thunderstorm.

questions.question: Norwesters normally occur during
questions.explanation: Peak daytime heating typically triggers norwesters in the afternoon.

questions.question: Norwesters originates over
questions.explanation: Norwesters characteristically originate over the Chota-Nagpur plateau region.

questions.question: Andhi (blinding storms) occur generally over
questions.explanation: Andhi (severe dust storms) are a Northern India, pre-monsoon phenomenon.

questions.question: Wind speed in Light DS is
questions.explanation: A light duststorm is defined by wind speeds up to about 21 kt.

questions.question: The diametre of Microburst is
questions.explanation: A microburst is defined as a small, intense downdraft with a diameter under 4 km.

questions.question: The diametre of and Macroburst
questions.explanation: A macroburst is the larger counterpart to a microburst, with a diameter of 4 km or more.

questions.question: For detecting precipitation a Radar wavelength in the range ........... is suitable
questions.explanation: Weather radars for precipitation detection commonly operate at wavelengths in the 30-200 mm range.

questions.question: For airborne radars wavelength generally used
questions.explanation: Airborne weather radars commonly operate around a 60 mm (roughly X-band) wavelength.

questions.question: The wavelength of TS detection X band radar is
questions.explanation: X-band thunderstorm detection radar operates at roughly 30 mm wavelength.

questions.question: The wavelength of storm detection S band radar is
questions.explanation: S-band storm detection radar uses a longer wavelength, around 100 mm, offering better penetration through heavy precipitation.

questions.question: Over plains TS mostly occur during the
questions.explanation: Surface heating drives thunderstorm development over plains typically in the afternoon.

questions.question: Over valley and foot hills TS generally occur during
questions.explanation: Katabatic drainage and convergence effects in valleys/foothills favour thunderstorm activity at night and early morning.

questions.question: Over the sea TS are more frequent
questions.explanation: Over the sea, the surface remains relatively warmer than the air aloft at night, favouring nighttime thunderstorm activity.

questions.question: The life of Mesoscale Convective Complex TS is
questions.explanation: A Mesoscale Convective Complex is a long-lived system that can persist from 6 up to 24 hours.

questions.question: Loud peals of thunder, frequent flashes of lightning, moderate or heavy showers accompanied by light hail with maximum wind speed 15-40 kt is classified as
questions.explanation: This intensity description matches the criteria for a moderate thunderstorm.

questions.question: For a severe TS one of the requirements is strong Wind Shear
questions.explanation: Strong vertical wind shear is a key ingredient supporting severe, long-lived thunderstorm development.

questions.question: Severe TS cells are tilted
questions.explanation: Severe thunderstorm cells are typically tilted in the vertical due to wind shear, separating updraft and downdraft regions.

questions.question: When flying through on active TS, lighting strikes are most likely
options: Above 5000 ft and under the anvil.
In the clear air below the cloud in rain
In the temperature band between +10° and - 10°C
questions.explanation: Lightning strikes are statistically most probable in the temperature band roughly between +10°C and -10°C within the storm.

questions.question: Hazards of the mature stage of a TS Cell include lighting, turbulence and:
questions.explanation: The mature stage brings the combined hazards of icing, microbursts, and wind shear alongside lightning and turbulence.

questions.question: Hail grows by
options: freezing as it leaves the cloud
up and down forces in CU cloud
questions.explanation: Hailstones grow through repeated collisions with supercooled water droplets that freeze on contact as the stone is carried up and down within the storm.

chapters.name: Air Masses, Fronts and Western Disturbances

questions.question: The airmass which originates at sea in high Latitudes is called
questions.explanation: An air mass forming over the sea at high latitudes is classified as Polar Maritime.

questions.question: The airmass which originates over equatorial region is
questions.explanation: Equatorial air masses form over warm, moisture-rich oceanic/tropical regions, so they are warm and moist.

questions.question: If the advancing cold front is colder than the cool air mass of the warm front, the advancing cold front undercuts and lifts both the warm and cool air masses of the warm front. This is
questions.explanation: When the advancing cold air is colder than the pre-existing cool air, it undercuts both other air masses, forming a cold occlusion.

questions.question: The airmass which originated over land area located in polar region is
questions.explanation: An air mass forming over cold, dry polar land is classified Continental Polar - cold and dry.

questions.question: If a warm airmass overtakes a cold air mass, it is called
questions.explanation: A warm front is defined as warm air actively advancing over and displacing cold air.

questions.question: At warm front
options: Warm air overtakes the cold air
Cold air undercuts the warm air
questions.explanation: This is the definition of a warm front.

questions.question: The conditions are always unstable at a
questions.explanation: The steep frontal slope and rapid lifting at a cold front typically produce unstable, showery conditions.

questions.question: Sometimes Line squall occurs about 100-300 km ahead of a
questions.explanation: Pre-frontal line squalls can develop 100-300 km ahead of an advancing cold front.

questions.question: Precipitation occurs over a belt of 30 - 50 km on both side of front
questions.explanation: The narrower precipitation zone (30-50 km either side) is typical of the steeper cold front, compared to the much broader warm-front precipitation band.

questions.question: Cold front moves at ... the speed of a warm front moves
questions.explanation: Cold fronts generally advance roughly twice as fast as warm fronts.

questions.question: Line Squalls occur ...... of Cold front
questions.explanation: Line squalls typically develop ahead of an advancing cold front.

questions.question: Fronts are associated with
questions.explanation: Fronts are a defining feature of extra-tropical (mid-latitude) cyclones, unlike tropical systems which lack fronts.

questions.question: CB, Roll-type clouds, SC, AC with embedded CB are associated
questions.explanation: These vigorous, convective cloud types are characteristic of a cold front passage.

questions.question: The surface of discontinuity between the Polar Ely and the temperate Wly is called
questions.explanation: The boundary between cold polar easterlies and the milder mid-latitude westerlies is termed the polar front.

questions.question: The air mass which originates from sea area located in lower Lat is
questions.explanation: An air mass originating over the sea at low (tropical) latitudes is warm and moist - Tropical Maritime.

questions.question: WDs approach India as
questions.explanation: Western Disturbances arrive as weakening, occluded frontal systems from the Mediterranean/Caspian region.

questions.question: Maximum WDs occur in
questions.explanation: Western Disturbances are most frequent and active during the winter season over North India.

questions.question: Ahead of a warm front the surface wind
questions.explanation: As a warm front approaches, the surface wind typically veers and strengthens.

questions.question: On approach of a Warm Front temperature
questions.explanation: Warm air replacing cold air ahead of a warm front causes temperature to rise.

questions.question: CI, CS, AS, NS, ST in sequence are associated with the front
questions.explanation: This progressive lowering/thickening cloud sequence (CI to CS to AS to NS to ST) is the classic warm front cloud progression.

questions.question: During the passage of a Cold Front winds
options: Veer and are of moderate strength
questions.explanation: The passage of a cold front typically brings a sudden, squally wind shift.

questions.question: Visibility is poor in a Warm Front
questions.explanation: Poor visibility (due to precipitation and low cloud) persists both ahead of and during warm front passage.

questions.question: Fog occurs in Cold Front
questions.explanation: Fog is more commonly associated with the period after a cold front has passed, as the air stabilises.

questions.question: WD is a ........... front
questions.explanation: By the time a Western Disturbance reaches India it typically has an occluded frontal structure.

questions.question: FZRA and FZFG occur ........... of a warm front
questions.explanation: Freezing rain and freezing fog commonly occur ahead of an approaching warm front, in the cold air below the frontal surface.

questions.question: Precipitation ceases after the passage of a front
questions.explanation: After a warm front passes, precipitation generally clears as warmer, more stable air moves in.

questions.question: During the approach of a Warm Front wind
questions.explanation: As a warm front approaches, the surface wind typically backs ahead of the eventual veer at frontal passage.

questions.question: A WD with two or more closed isobars, at 2 hPa interval, it is termed as
questions.explanation: A more developed WD with two or more closed 2 hPa isobars is classified as a Western Depression.

questions.question: A WD originate over
questions.explanation: Western Disturbances originate over the Mediterranean, Caspian, and Black Sea regions before tracking eastward toward India.

questions.question: Induced lows develop to the ........ of a WD
questions.explanation: Induced (secondary) lows commonly develop to the south of an approaching Western Disturbance, often over Rajasthan/Punjab plains.

questions.question: The arbitrary lower limit of jet core velocity has been assigned by WMO as
questions.explanation: WMO's arbitrary threshold defining a jet stream core is a wind speed of at least 60 kt.

questions.question: Jet stream has
questions.explanation: A jet stream can contain one or several localized speed maxima (jet streaks) along its axis.

questions.question: The vertical wind shear in a Jet stream is about
questions.explanation: Typical vertical wind shear within a jet stream is on the order of 5 m/s per km.

questions.question: Compared to horizontal wind shear the vertical wind shear in a Jet stream is
questions.explanation: Vertical wind shear across a jet stream is generally much stronger than the horizontal shear.

questions.question: In a jet stream, the path of the maximum speed is known as
questions.explanation: The line tracing the maximum wind speed through a jet stream is called its axis.

questions.question: The wind speed along the axis of a jet stream is always
questions.explanation: Wind speed varies along the jet axis, with localized maxima called jet streaks.

questions.question: Along the axis of a jet stream there are centres of high speed winds, these are called
questions.explanation: Jet streaks are the localized regions of maximum wind speed along a jet stream's axis.

questions.question: In a wavy jet the Jet streaks are located over or near the
questions.explanation: In a meandering (wavy) jet stream, streaks of maximum wind commonly occur near the ridge.

questions.question: Sub-tropical Jet Stream (STJ) is
questions.explanation: The subtropical jet stream flows from west to east.

questions.question: The normal position of Sub-tropical Jet Stream is
questions.explanation: The STJ is typically positioned around 27°N.

questions.question: The southern most position of STJ is in February is
questions.explanation: The STJ reaches its southernmost extent, around 22°N, in February.

questions.question: The STJ affects India from
questions.explanation: The subtropical jet influences India during the cooler months, roughly October through May.

questions.question: STJ has a layered structure. There are often two layers of max wind to the ........ of jet core
questions.explanation: The STJ can show two vertically stacked wind maxima, generally to the south of the main jet core.

questions.question: The STJ strengthens
questions.explanation: The subtropical jet tends to intensify further downstream (eastward) along its track.

questions.question: At and near the STJ the temperature gradient is very
questions.explanation: Near the jet core itself the horizontal temperature gradient is relatively weak, being strongest on the polar side.

questions.question: Vertical wind shear in STJ is greater ........... the core
questions.explanation: Vertical wind shear associated with the subtropical jet is generally stronger above the jet core than below it.

questions.question: The TJ prevails over the Indian Peninsula from
questions.explanation: The Tropical Easterly Jet is present over the Indian Peninsula during the monsoon months, June to August.

questions.question: The TJ is located over the Indian Peninsula, approximately at
questions.explanation: The Tropical Jet axis over India lies around 13°N.

questions.question: The TJ is located over Indian, approximately at a height of
questions.explanation: The Tropical Easterly Jet is found at a relatively high altitude, roughly 15-16 km, over India.

questions.question: The TJ is strongest in
questions.explanation: The Tropical Easterly Jet reaches peak strength during the core monsoon months of July-August.

questions.question: In the TJ the wind shears are much ........... than the STJ
questions.explanation: Wind shear associated with the Tropical Jet is generally weaker than that of the subtropical jet.

questions.question: TJ is
questions.explanation: The Tropical Jet is an easterly (blowing from east to west) upper-level current.

questions.question: A jet stream can be recognized by
questions.explanation: Bands of cirrus cloud streaking along the flow are a common visual indicator of a jet stream.

questions.question: Flying at right angles to a jet stream with falling pressure you will experience
questions.explanation: Applying the pressure-wind relationship (N hemisphere, low pressure to the left of the wind) while crossing the jet at right angles with falling pressure implies the wind is coming from the left.

questions.question: When and where tropical jet stream occurs
options: In summers over SE Asia and Central Africa
questions.explanation: The Tropical Easterly Jet develops during the summer monsoon season, extending across Southeast Asia and Central Africa.

questions.question: For mountain waves to form there should be flow of air across the ridge, generally within ........... of the perpendicular to the ridge.
questions.explanation: Effective mountain wave formation requires wind flow within about 30° of perpendicular to the ridge line.

questions.question: For mountain waves to form the wind speed for small mountains should be atleast
questions.explanation: Smaller mountain ranges can generate waves with a minimum wind speed of about 7 m/s.

questions.question: For mountain waves to form the wind speed for large mountains should be atleast
questions.explanation: Larger mountain ranges require a stronger minimum wind speed, around 15 m/s, to generate waves.

questions.question: For mountain waves to form there should be ..... air below the ridge and less stable air above.
questions.explanation: A stable layer near ridge height with less stable air above favours the formation of a resonant mountain wave.

questions.question: The worst kind of turbulence is encountered in the vicinity of rotor clouds.
questions.explanation: The turbulent rotor circulation beneath a mountain wave, marked by rotor clouds, produces the most severe turbulence.

questions.question: In Mountain waves the Rotor clouds form in
questions.explanation: Rotor clouds typically form over the ridge/crest regions of the mountain wave circulation.

questions.question: Clear air turbulence is often encountered
options: At the boundary of a jet stream
In the wake of a passing airplane
In the wake of a larger airplane at take off and landing
questions.explanation: CAT is most commonly associated with strong wind shear at the edges of a jet stream.

questions.question: Most CAT occurs on the ........... of a jet stream and in the vicinity of upper level frontal zones where temperature contrasts are strong.
questions.explanation: The strongest shear, and hence most CAT, occurs on the fringes of the jet rather than within its core.

questions.question: CAT is the bumpiness experienced by aircraft at high altitudes. Over North India its maximum frequency is during
questions.explanation: CAT frequency over North India peaks during the cooler months (Oct-May) when the subtropical jet is active.

questions.question: When approaching an area where mountain waves have been reported, a pilot should expect:
options: Possible presence of roll clouds and lenticular clouds
Intense up draughts and down draughts on the lee side of the mountains.
Moderate to severe turbulence as far as 20 to 30 nm from range on leeward side.
questions.explanation: Mountain wave areas can produce all of these effects together - lenticular/roll clouds, strong vertical currents, and turbulence extending well downstream.

questions.question: Wind speed in a tropical severe cyclone is:
questions.explanation: A severe cyclonic storm is classified by sustained wind speeds in the range of roughly 48-63 kt.

questions.question: Fronts are characteristic of:

An aircraft's mass is a result of:
questions.explanation: Mass is a measure of the amount of matter an object contains (atoms and molecules), unlike weight, which is a force.

questions.question: The unit of mass is the:
questions.explanation: The kilogram (kg) is the SI unit of mass.

questions.question: The definition of a force is:
options: That which causes a reaction to take place.
The result of an applied input
questions.explanation: In physics, force is defined as a push or pull upon an object resulting from its interaction with another object; it can change an object's speed, direction, or shape.

questions.question: The unit of force is the
questions.explanation: Force = mass x acceleration (F = m x a). Multiplying kg by m/s2 gives the Newton, the SI unit of force (1 N = 1 kg.m/s2).

questions.question: The unit of weight is the
questions.explanation: Weight is a force (Weight = Mass x g), so it is measured in Newtons, the same unit as any other force.

questions.question: Weight is the result of:
options: The force on mass due to gravity
The action of a falling mass
How much matter the object contains
The rate of mass per unit area
questions.explanation: Weight is the force produced when an object's mass is acted on by gravitational acceleration (Weight = Mass x g).

questions.question: About which point does an aircraft rotate:
questions.explanation: The centre of gravity is the point at which the aircraft's weight is balanced in all directions, and it acts as the pivot point for pitch, roll, and yaw.

questions.question: If a force is applied to a mass and the mass does not move:
options: Work is done even through there is no movement of the mass
Work is done only if the mass moves a long way
Power is exerted, but no work is done
questions.explanation: Work = Force x displacement. If the object does not move, displacement is zero, so the work done is zero.

questions.question: The unit of work is called the:
questions.explanation: Work is force multiplied by displacement in the direction of the force. The SI unit of work is the Joule (J), where 1 J = 1 N.m.

questions.question: The unit of power is called the:
questions.explanation: Power is the rate of doing work (Power = Work / Time), and its SI unit is the Watt (W).

questions.question: If a force of 20 Newton's moves a mass 5 metres: 1-The work done is 100Nm 2-The work done is 100 Joules 3-The work done is 4 Joules 4-The work done is 0.25 Joules The correct statements are:
questions.explanation: Work = Force x distance = 20 N x 5 m = 100 Nm = 100 Joules (1 Nm = 1 Joule of work), so both statements 1 and 2 are correct.

questions.question: If a force of 50 Newton's is applied to a 10 kg mass and the mass moves 10 metres and a force of 50 Newton's is applied to a 100kg mass which moves 10 metres:
options: The work done is the same in both cases
Less work is done to the 10 kg mass
More work is done to the 10 kg mass
More work is done to the 100 kg mass
questions.explanation: Work depends only on force and displacement (W = F x d), not on the mass being moved, so with equal force and equal displacement the work done is identical in both cases.

questions.question: The definition of power is:
options: The rate of movement per second
questions.explanation: Power is defined as the rate at which work is done (Power = Work / Time).

questions.question: If a force of 500 Newton's moves a mass 1000 metres in 2 mins, the power used is:
questions.explanation: Power = (Force x distance) / time = (500 x 1000) / 120 seconds = 4167 Watts.

questions.question: Kinetic energy is:
options: The energy a mass possesses due ti its position in space
The energy a mass possesses when a force has been applied
The energy a mass possesses due to the force of gravity
The energy a mass possesses because of its motion
