questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is the energy an object possesses due to its motion, given by KE = 1/2 mv2.

questions.question: The unit of kinetic energy is the:
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is a form of energy, and the SI unit of energy is the Joule (J).

questions.question: When considering kinetic energy: 1-a moving mass can apply a force by being brought to rest. 2-kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body because of its motion. 3-if a body's kinetic energy is increased, a force must have been applied. 4-kinetic energy = 1/2 m V2 joules. The combination of correct statement is:
questions.explanation: All four statements are valid descriptions of kinetic energy and how it relates to force and motion, so all are correct.

questions.question: The property of inertia is said to be:
options: The energy possessed by a body because of its motion
The opposition which a body offers to a change in motion
That every action has an equal and opposite reaction
The quantity of motion possessed by a body
questions.explanation: Inertia is the fundamental property of matter that resists any change in its state of motion or rest, as described by Newton's First Law of Motion.

questions.question: Considering Newton's first law of motion: 1-a body is said to have energy if it has the ability to do work. 2-The amount of energy a body possesses is measured by the amount of work it can do. 3-a body will tend to remain at rest, or in uniform motion in a straight line, unless acted upon by an external force. 4-to move a stationary object or to make a moving object changes its direction, a force must be applied. The combination with the correct statements is:
questions.explanation: Statements 3 and 4 describe Newton's First Law; statements 1 and 2, while true, relate to energy and work rather than the First Law itself.

questions.question: Considering Newton's second law of motion: 1- every action has an equal and opposite reaction. 2-If the same force is applied, the larger the mass the slower the acceleration. 3-If two forces are applied to the same mass, the bigger the force the greater the acceleration. 4-the acceleration of a body from a state of rest, or uniform motion in a straight line, is proportional to the applied force and inversely proportional to the mass. The combination of true statements is:
questions.explanation: Statements 2, 3 and 4 correctly describe Newton's Second Law; statement 1 is incorrect because it actually belongs to Newton's Third Law.

questions.question: Newton's third law of motion states:
options: The energy possessed by a mass is inversely proportional to its velocity
Every force has an equal and opposite inertia
For every force there is an action.
Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
questions.explanation: Newton's Third Law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction (F(action) = -F(reaction)).

questions.question: The definition of velocity is the:
options: The quantity of motion possessed by a body
The acceleration of a body in direct proportion to its mass
questions.explanation: Velocity is defined as the displacement covered by an object per unit time in a particular direction (v = d/t).

questions.question: When considering acceleration: 1-acceleration is the rate of change of velocity 2-the units of acceleration are metres per second 3-the units of acceleration are kilogram-metres per second. 4-the units of acceleration are seconds per metre per metre. The combination of correct statements is:
questions.explanation: Acceleration is correctly defined as the rate of change of velocity (statement 1); its correct SI unit is metres per second squared (m/s2), not the units given in statements 2, 3, or 4.

questions.question: The definition of momentum is:
options: The quantity of mass possessed by a body.
The quantity of inertia possessed by a body.
The quantity of motion possessed by a body.
The opposition which a body offers to a change in velocity
questions.explanation: Momentum is defined as the product of an object's mass and velocity (momentum = mass x velocity), measuring the quantity of motion a body possesses.

questions.question: A force of 24 Newton's moves a 10 kg mass 60 metres in 1 minute, the power used is? 1-24 Watts 2-240 Watts. 3-Force times distance moved in one second. 4-Force times the distance the mass is moved in one second. Which of the preceding statements are correct
questions.explanation: Power = (Force x distance) / time = (24 N x 60 m) / 60 s = 24 Watts, which matches statement 1; statements 3 and 4 correctly describe how that power is calculated (force times distance moved per second).

questions.question: When considering momentum: 1- Momentum is the quantity of motion possessed by a body. 2-Momentum is the tendency of a body to continue in motion after being placed in motion. 3-A mass of 2000 kg moving at 55 m/s has momentum. 4-A large mass moving at 50 m/s will have less momentum than a small mass moving at 50 m/s. The correct combination of statement is:
questions.explanation: Momentum = mass x velocity, so statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct; statement 4 is wrong because at the same velocity a larger mass has greater, not less, momentum.

questions.question: When considering air: 1- Air has mass 2- Air is not compressible 3-Air is able to flow or change its shape when subject to even small pressures 4-The viscosity of air is very high 5-Moving air has kinetic energy. The correct combination of all true statements is:
questions.explanation: Air has mass and moving air has kinetic energy, and it flows or changes shape readily under even very small pressure differences. Air is compressible (not incompressible) and has very low, not high, viscosity, so statements 2 and 4 are false.

questions.question: Why do the lower the layers contain the greater proportion of the whole mass of the atmosphere:
options: Because of greater levels of humidity at low altitude
Because air has very little mass
questions.explanation: Since air is compressible, the weight of the air above squeezes and densifies the air below, so most of the atmosphere's mass is concentrated in the lower layers.

questions.question: With increasing altitude, up to about 40,000 ft, the characteristics of air change: 1 - Temperature decreases continuously with altitude 2 - Pressure falls steadily to an altitude of about 36,000 ft, where it then remains constant 3 - Density decreases steadily with increasing altitude 4 - Pressure falls steadily with increasing altitude The combination of true statements is:
questions.explanation: Density and pressure both fall steadily with increasing altitude (statements 3 and 4). Statement 1 is wrong because temperature only falls steadily up to about 36,000 ft and is then constant, and statement 2 is wrong because it is temperature, not pressure, that levels off at that height.

questions.question: When considering static pressure: 1-In aviation, static pressure can be measured in hectopascals 2-The SI units for static pressure is N/m² 3-Static pressure is the product of the mass of air pressing down on the air beneath 4-Referred to as static pressure because of the air's stationary or static presence 5-The lower the altitude, the greater the static pressure. The correct statements are:
questions.explanation: All five statements correctly describe static pressure: its units (hectopascals, N/m2), its cause (the weight of the air column above pressing down), why it is called "static", and the fact that it increases as altitude decreases.

questions.question: When considering air density: 1-Density is measured in millibars 2-Density increases with increasing altitude 3-If temperature increases the density will increase 4-As altitude increases, density will decrease 5-Temperature decreases with increasing altitude, this will cause air density to increase. The combination of correct statement is:
questions.explanation: Only statement 4 is correct: density decreases as altitude increases. Density is measured in kg/m3, not millibars; density decreases (not increases) with altitude; density is inversely, not directly, proportional to temperature; and although temperature falls with altitude, the overall effect of increasing altitude is a decrease, not an increase, in density.

questions.question: Air density is:
options: Proportional to temperature and inversely proportional to pressure
Independent of both temperature and pressure
Dependent only on decreasing pressure with increasing altitude.
questions.explanation: Density is defined as mass per unit volume. From the ideal gas relationship, density is actually proportional to pressure and inversely proportional to temperature, not the reverse, and it depends on both quantities together, not on pressure alone.

questions.question: When considering the ICAO International Standard Atmosphere and comparing it with the actual atmosphere, which of the following statements is correct: 1-Temperature, pressure and density are constantly changing in any given layer of the actual atmosphere. 2-A requirement exists for a hypothetical 'standard' atmosphere. 3-The values given in the International Standard Atmosphere exist at a the same altitudes in the actual atmosphere. 4-The International Standard Atmosphere was designed for the calibration of pressure instruments and the comparison of aircraft performance calculations
questions.explanation: The real atmosphere constantly varies (statement 1), which is why a fixed reference model is needed (statement 2) for calibrating instruments and comparing performance (statement 4). Statement 3 is false because the ISA is only a theoretical model, and its values rarely match the real atmosphere at the same altitude.

questions.question: When considering the ICAO International Standard Atmosphere, which of the following statements is correct: 1-The temperature lapse rate is assumed to be uniform at 2°C per 1,000 ft (1.98°C) up to a height of 11,000 ft. 2-Sea level temperature is assumed to be 15°C 3-Sea level static pressure is assumed to be 1.225 kg/m³ 4-Sea level density is assumed to be 1013.25 hPa
questions.explanation: Only statement 2 is correct: ISA sea level temperature is defined as 15°C. Statements 3 and 4 have the units swapped - sea level density is 1.225 kg/m3 and sea level pressure is 1013.25 hPa - and the ISA lapse rate up to 11,000 m (not 11,000 ft) is close to but not exactly as stated.

questions.question: A moving mass of air possesses kinetic energy. An object placed in the path of such a moving mass of air will be subject to which of the following:
questions.explanation: An object in a moving airstream experiences the surrounding static pressure of the air plus the additional dynamic pressure generated by bringing the moving air to rest against it.

questions.question: Dynamic pressure is:
options: The total pressure at a point where a moving airflow is brought completely to rest.
The amount by which the pressure rises at a point where a moving airflow is brought completely to rest.
The pressure due to the mass of air pressing down on the air beneath
The pressure change caused by heating when a moving airflow is brought completely to rest.
questions.explanation: Dynamic pressure is the additional rise in pressure above the static pressure that occurs when moving air is brought to rest, rather than the total pressure itself.

questions.question: Dynamic pressure is equal to:
options: Half the density times the indicated airspeed squared
Half the true airspeed times the density squared
Half the density times the true airspeed squared
questions.explanation: Dynamic pressure follows the formula q = 1/2 x density x (true airspeed)^2, where density and velocity are correctly ordered in the equation.

questions.question: A tube facing into an airflow will experience a pressure in the tube equal to:
options: The difference between total pressure and static pressure
questions.explanation: A tube facing directly into the airflow (a pitot tube) senses total pressure, which by Bernoulli's principle equals the static pressure of the surrounding air plus the dynamic pressure generated by bringing the air to rest.

questions.question: A static pressure vent must be positioned:
options: On a part of the aircraft structure where the airflow is undisturbed, in a surface at right angles to the airflow direction.
On a part of the structure where the airflow is undisturbed, in a surface parallel to the airflow direction.
At the point on the surface where the airflow reaches the highest speed
questions.explanation: A static vent must sit where the airflow is undisturbed and lie in a surface parallel to the airflow, so that it senses only static pressure without picking up any dynamic pressure component.

questions.question: The inputs to an Airspeed Indicator are from:
options: A pitot and a static source
questions.explanation: The Airspeed Indicator compares total pressure sensed at the pitot tube with static pressure sensed at the static source; the difference between the two drives the airspeed reading.

questions.question: The deflection of the pointer of the Air Speed Indicator is proportional to:
options: The difference between static and dynamic pressure
questions.explanation: The capsule inside the Airspeed Indicator expands and contracts according to dynamic pressure (total pressure minus static pressure), and this movement drives the pointer.

questions.question: Calibration of the Air Speed Indicator is based upon the density:
options: At the altitude at which the aircraft is flying.
At sea level ICAO International Standard Atmosphere temperature
At sea level ICAO International Standard Atmosphere +15°C temperature
questions.explanation: The Airspeed Indicator is calibrated using the density corresponding to ICAO ISA sea level temperature conditions, giving a fixed reference so that airspeed readings are consistent regardless of the aircraft's actual altitude.

questions.question: When considering the relationship between different types of air speed: 1-True Air Speed (TAS) is read directly from the Air Speed Indicator. 2-Equivalent Air Speed is Indicated Air Speed corrected for position error 3-Indicated Air Speed is not a speed at all, it's a pressure 4- True Air Speed is the Speed of the aircraft through the air. Which of the above statements are true:
questions.explanation: Statement 3 is correct because Indicated Airspeed is essentially a dynamic pressure measurement displayed as a speed, and statement 4 correctly defines True Airspeed as the aircraft's actual speed through the air mass. Statement 1 is wrong because the indicator displays Indicated Airspeed, not TAS directly, and statement 2 is wrong because Equivalent Airspeed corrects for compressibility, not position error.

questions.question: When considering the relationship between different types of air speed: 1-Calibrated AirSpeed is Indicated Airspeed corrected for position error 2-Equivalent Air Speed is Indicated Air Speed corrected for position error and compressibility 3-Position error, which causes false Indicated Airspeed readings, is due to variations in the pressures sensed at the pitot and static ports. 4-The Air Speed Indicator is calibrated to read True Air Speed when the ambient density is that of the ICAO International Standard Atmosphere at sea level. The combination of correct statements is:
options: Non of the statements are correct
questions.explanation: Calibrated Airspeed corrects Indicated Airspeed for position error, Equivalent Airspeed further corrects for compressibility, position error itself stems from inaccurate pressure sensing at the pitot and static ports, and the indicator is calibrated to read True Airspeed under ICAO ISA sea level density conditions, making all four statements correct.

questions.question: The speed of sound:
options: Is dependent upon the True Air Speed and the Mach number of the aircraft.
Is inversely proportional to the absolute temperature.
Is proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature of the air
Is directly proportional to the True Air Speed of the aircraft
questions.explanation: Sound travels as pressure waves whose propagation speed depends on the square root of the absolute temperature of the air; the lower the temperature, the slower the speed of sound, and it is unrelated to the aircraft's own speed.

questions.question: Mach number is:
options: The aircraft True Air Speed divided by the local speed of sound
The speed of sound in the ambient conditions in which the aircraft is flying
The True Air Speed of the aircraft at which the relative airflow somewhere on the aircraft first reaches the local speed of sound
The Indicated Air Speed divided by the local speed of sound sea level
questions.explanation: Mach number is the ratio of the aircraft's True Airspeed to the local speed of sound at the altitude the aircraft is flying at.

questions.question: An aircraft's critical Mach number is;
options: The speed of the airflow when the aircraft first becomes supersonic
The Speed of the aircraft when the airflow somewhere reaches the speed of sound
The Indicated Airspeed when the aircraft first becomes supersonic
The aircraft's Mach number when airflow over it first reaches the local speed of sound
questions.explanation: The critical Mach number is the aircraft's Mach number at which airflow over some part of the aircraft, typically the point of maximum thickness on the wing, first reaches the local speed of sound, even though the aircraft itself is still flying at a subsonic speed.

questions.question: If the cross sectional area of an airflow is mechanically reduced:
options: The velocity of the airflow remains constant and the kinetic energy increases
The velocity of the airflow remains constant and the mass flow increases
The mass flow remains constant and the static pressure increases
The mass flow remains constant and the velocity of the airflow increases
questions.explanation: By the principle of continuity, mass flow through a duct must stay constant. When the cross-sectional area is reduced, the airflow must speed up to keep the same mass flowing per second.

questions.question: The statement, "pressure plus kinetic energy is constant", refers to:
questions.explanation: Bernoulli's theorem states that in a steady, incompressible flow, the sum of pressure energy and kinetic energy along a streamline remains constant, so if velocity (kinetic energy) increases, static pressure must decrease, and vice versa.

questions.question: If the velocity of an air mass is increased:
options: The dynamic pressure will decrease and the static pressure will increase
The static pressure will remain constant and the kinetic energy will increase
The kinetic energy will increase, the dynamic pressure will increase and the static pressure will decrease
The mass flow will stay constant, the dynamic pressure will decrease and the static pressure will increase
questions.explanation: An increase in airflow velocity raises both kinetic energy and dynamic pressure; by Bernoulli's theorem, since total energy is constant, this rise is balanced by a corresponding fall in static pressure.

questions.question: When considering a streamlined airflow, which of the following statements is correct:
options: A resultant decrease in static pressure is indicated by streamlines shown close together
An increase in velocity is indicated by streamlines shown close together
Accelerating airflow with a resultant decreasing static pressure is indicated by converging streamlines
Diverging streamlines indicate decelerating airflow with a resultant increasing static pressure
questions.explanation: Where streamlines diverge (spread apart), the airflow is decelerating, and by Bernoulli's theorem this deceleration is accompanied by a rise in static pressure.

questions.question: If the pressure on one side of a surface is lower than on the other side:
options: A force per unit area will exist, acting in the direction of the lower pressure
No force will be generated, other than drag
A force will be generated, acting in the direction of the higher pressure
The pressure will leak around the sides of the surface, cancelling-out any pressure differential
questions.explanation: A pressure difference across a surface produces a net force per unit area that acts from the region of higher pressure toward the region of lower pressure.

questions.question: When considering a streamtube, which of the following statements is correct:
options: Different sizes of streamtube are manufactured to match the wing span of the aircraft to which they will be fitted
A streamtube is a concept to aid understanding of aerodynamic force generation
There is no flow into or out of the streamtube through the "walls", only flow along the tube
A streamtube is an imaginary tube made-up of streamlines
questions.explanation: A streamtube is bounded by streamlines, and since air cannot cross a streamline, no air flows through its "walls" - all flow moves along the length of the tube.

questions.question: In accordance with the principle of continuity: 1. air accelerates when the cross-sectional area of a streamline flow is reduced. 2. when air accelerates the density of air in a streamline flow is increased. 3. air decelerates when the cross-sectional area of a streamline flow is increased. 4. changes in cross-sectional area of a streamline flow will affect the air velocity. Which of the preceding statements are true?
questions.explanation: Statements 1, 3 and 4 correctly describe the principle of continuity: reducing the cross-sectional area accelerates the flow, increasing it decelerates the flow, and any change in area affects velocity. Statement 2 is incorrect because, for a low-speed, effectively incompressible flow, density remains constant rather than increasing when air accelerates.

questions.question: In accordance with the principle of continuity:
options: Air accelerates when the cross-sectional area of a streamline flow is reduced
When air accelerates the density of air in a streamline flow is increased
Air decelerates when the cross-sectional area of a streamline flow is increased
Changes in cross-sectional area of a streamline flow will affect the air velocity
questions.explanation: The principle of continuity is best summarised by the statement that any change in the cross-sectional area of a streamline flow affects the velocity of the air, since mass flow must remain constant.

questions.question: In accordance with Bernoulli's theorem:
options: If a streamline flow of air decelerates, its kinetic energy will decrease and the static pressure will increase
If a streamline flow of air accelerates, its kinetic energy will increase and the static pressure will decrease
If a streamline flow of air is accelerated, the dynamic pressure will increase and the static pressure will increase
If a streamline flow of air is decelerated, its dynamic pressure will decrease and the static pressure will increase
questions.explanation: Bernoulli's theorem states that the sum of static and dynamic pressure along a streamline is constant, so when a flow accelerates, its kinetic energy and dynamic pressure rise while its static pressure falls. Note: the source material did not clearly mark which option was scored correct for this question - options a and d are also internally consistent with Bernoulli's theorem, so it's worth double-checking this one against your reference text.

questions.question: The statement, "Energy and mass can neither be created nor destroyed, only changed from one form to another", refers to:
questions.explanation: This statement describes the conservation of mass and energy, which is the underlying physical basis for the principle of continuity in fluid flow.

questions.question: With reference to aerofoil section terminology, which of the following statements is true:
options: The chord line is a line joining the centre of curvature of the leading edge to the centre of the trailing edge, equidistant from the top and bottom surface of the aerofoil.
The angle of incidence is the angle between the chord line and the horizontal datum of the aircraft.
The angle between the chord line and the relative airflow is called the aerodynamic incidence or angle of attack.
The thickness/chord ratio is the maximum thickness of the aerofoil as a percentage of the chord; the location of maximum thickness is measured as a percentage of the chord aft of the leading edge.
questions.explanation: The angle between the chord line and the relative airflow is known as the aerodynamic incidence or angle of attack.

questions.question: The definition of lift is:
options: The aerodynamic force which acts perpendicular to the chord line of the aerofoil.
The aerodynamic force that results from the pressure differentials about an aerofoil.
The aerodynamic force which acts perpendicular to the upper surface of the aerofoil.
The aerodynamic force which acts at 90° to the relative airflow.
questions.explanation: Lift is defined as the aerodynamic force acting perpendicular to the relative airflow.

questions.question: An aerofoil section is designed to produce lift resulting from a difference in the:
options: Negative air pressure below and a vacuum above the surface.
Vacuum below the surface and greater air pressure above the surface.
Higher air pressure below the surface and lower air pressure above the surface.
Higher air pressure below the surface and lower air pressure above the surface.
questions.explanation: Lift is produced by higher pressure beneath the aerofoil and lower pressure above it.

questions.question: On an aerofoil section, the force of lift acts perpendicular to, and the force of drag acts parallel to the:
questions.explanation: Lift acts perpendicular to the relative airflow (flightpath), while drag acts parallel to it.

questions.question: When the angle of attack of a symmetrical aerofoil is increased, the centre of pressure will:
options: Move aft along the aerofoil surface.
Move forward to the leading edge.
questions.explanation: For a symmetrical aerofoil, the centre of pressure remains essentially unchanged with changes in angle of attack.

questions.question: Why does increasing speed also increase lift?
options: The increased impact of the relative wind on an aerofoil's lower surface creates a greater amount of air being deflected downward.
The increased speed of the air passing over an aerofoil's surface decreases the static pressure, thus creating a greater pressure differential between the upper and lower surface.
The increased velocity of the relative wind overcomes the increased drag.
questions.explanation: Increasing airflow speed lowers static pressure over the aerofoil, increasing the pressure differential and therefore lift.

questions.question: The point on an aerofoil section through which lift acts is the:
questions.explanation: The resultant lift force acts through the centre of pressure.

questions.question: The angle between the chord line of the aerofoil section and the longitudinal axis of the aircraft is known as:
questions.explanation: The angle of incidence is the fixed angle between the chord line and the aircraft's longitudinal axis.

questions.question: The angle between the chord line of an aerofoil section and the relative wind is known as the angle of:
questions.explanation: Angle of attack is the angle between the chord line and the relative airflow.

questions.question: A line drawn from the leading edge to the trailing edge of an aerofoil section and equidistant at all points from the upper and lower contours is called the:
questions.explanation: The mean camber line is equidistant from the upper and lower surfaces throughout the aerofoil.

questions.question: At zero angle of attack, the pressure along the upper surface of a symmetrical aerofoil section would be:
questions.explanation: Air accelerates over the upper surface, producing pressure lower than atmospheric.

questions.question: The angle of attack of an aerofoil section directly controls:
options: Amount of airflow above and below the section.
Angle of incidence of the section.
Distribution of positive and negative pressure acting on the section.
The angle relative to the horizontal datum.
questions.explanation: Changing angle of attack alters the pressure distribution around the aerofoil.

questions.question: When the angle of attack of a positively cambered aerofoil is increased, the centre of pressure will:
options: Move forward along the chord line.
questions.explanation: For a cambered aerofoil, increasing angle of attack moves the centre of pressure forward.

questions.question: The term "angle of attack" is defined as the angle:
options: Formed by the longitudinal axis of the aeroplane and the chord line of the section.
Between the section chord line and the relative wind.
Between the aeroplane's climb angle and the horizon.
Formed by the leading edge of the section and the relative airflow.
questions.explanation: Angle of attack is the angle between the chord line and the relative airflow.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true:
options: Relative airflow, free stream flow, relative wind and aircraft flightpath are parallel.
Aircraft, flightpath, relative airflow, relative wind and free stream flow are parallel, but the aircraft flightpath is opposite in direction.
The pressure, temperature and relative velocity of the free stream flow are unaffected by the presence of the aircraft.
The relative wind is produced by the aircraft moving through the air.
questions.explanation: Relative wind is the airflow opposite to the aircraft's direction of travel.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct:
options: Maximum camber is the maximum distance between the top and bottom surface of an aerofoil section.
The thickness/chord ratio is expressed as a percentage of the chord.
It is easier for air to flow over a well rounded leading edge radius than a sharp leading edge.
Two dimensional airflow assumes a wing with the same aerofoil section along its entire span, with no spanwise pressure differential.
questions.explanation: Thickness-to-chord ratio is expressed as a percentage of the chord length.

questions.question: When considering an aerofoil section at a constant angle of attack, which of the following statements is true:
options: If the static pressure on one side is reduced more than on the other side, a pressure differential will exist.
If dynamic pressure is increased, the pressure differential will decrease.
The pressure differential will increase if the dynamic pressure is decreased.
Dynamic pressure and pressure differential are not related.
questions.explanation: A difference in static pressure between the two surfaces creates lift.

questions.question: Considering an aerofoil section subject to a constant dynamic pressure, which of the following statements is correct:
options: If the angle of attack is increased from 4° to 14° the pressure differential will not change but lift will be greater due to increased dynamic pressure acting on the lower surface.
Up to about 16°, increasing the angle of attack will increase the pressure differential between the top and bottom surface of the aerofoil.
Changing the angle of attack does not affect the pressure differential, only changes in dynamic pressure affect the pressure differential.
Up to about 16°, increasing the angle of attack decreases the pressure differential between the top and bottom surface of the aerofoil section.
questions.explanation: Increasing angle of attack up to the critical angle increases the pressure differential and lift.

questions.question: When considering the effect of changing angle of attack on the pitching moment of an aerofoil, which of the following statements is correct:
options: At normal angles of attack the pitching moment is nose up.
The pitching moment about the aerodynamic centre (AC) is constant at normal angles of attack.
The aerodynamic centre (AC) is located approximately at the 25% chord point.
The moment about the aerodynamic centre (AC) is the product of the distance between the aerodynamic centre (AC) and the centre of pressure (CP) and the magnitude of the lift force.
questions.explanation: The pitching moment depends on the lift force and the distance between the aerodynamic centre and the centre of pressure.

questions.question: Ice contamination of the leading portion of the aerofoil has which of the following consequences:
options: The profile of the leading portion of the surface can be changed, preventing normal acceleration of the airflow and substantially reducing the magnitude of the lift force.
Form (pressure) drag will be increased because of the increased frontal area of the aerofoil section.
Loss of lift will have a greater effect than an increase in form (pressure) drag.
At normal angles of attack lift can be lost entirely if enough ice accumulates.
questions.explanation: Ice distorts the aerofoil shape, disrupting airflow, reducing lift significantly, and increasing stall speed.

questions.question: To maintain altitude, what must be done as Indicated Air Speed (IAS) is reduced:
options: Decrease angle of attack to reduce the drag.
Increase angle of attack to maintain the correct lift force.
Deploy the speed brakes to increase drag.
questions.explanation: To maintain altitude as IAS decreases, the angle of attack must be increased to maintain sufficient lift.

questions.question: If more lift force is required because of greater operating weight, what must be done to fly at the angle of attack which corresponds to CLMAX:
options: Nothing, the angle of attack for CLMAX is constant.
It is impossible to fly at the angle of attack that corresponds to CLMAX.
questions.explanation: Since CLMAX occurs at a fixed angle of attack, a heavier aircraft requires a higher IAS to generate the required lift.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct: .1. To generate a constant lift force, any adjustment in IAS must be accompanied by a change in angle of attack. .2. For a constant lift force, each IAS requires a specific angle of attack. .3. Minimum IAS is determined by CLMAX. .4. The greater the operating weight, the higher the minimum IAS.
questions.explanation: All four statements are correct for steady level flight and lift generation.

questions.question: What effect does landing at high altitude airports have on ground speed with comparable conditions relative to temperature, wind, and aeroplane weight:
options: The same as at low altitude.
Dynamic pressure will be the same at any altitude.
questions.explanation: Higher altitude requires a higher true airspeed for the same IAS, resulting in a higher ground speed.

questions.question: What flight condition should be expected when an aircraft leaves ground effect:
options: A decrease in parasite drag permitting a lower angle of attack.
An increase in induced drag and a requirement for a higher angle of attack.
A decrease in induced drag requiring a smaller angle of attack.
questions.explanation: Leaving ground effect increases induced drag, requiring a higher angle of attack or more thrust.

questions.question: What will be the ratio between airspeed and lift if the angle of attack and other factors remain constant and airspeed is doubled. Lift will be:
questions.explanation: Lift varies with the square of airspeed, so doubling airspeed increases lift by four times.

questions.question: What true airspeed and angle of attack should be used to generate the same amount of lift as altitude is increased:
options: A higher true airspeed for any given angle of attack.
The same true airspeed and angle of attack.
A lower true airspeed and higher angle of attack.
A constant angle of attack and true airspeed.
questions.explanation: Reduced air density at higher altitude requires a higher TAS for the same angle of attack and lift.

questions.question: How can an aeroplane produce the same lift in ground effect as when out of ground effect:
options: The same angle of attack, but a lower IAS.
questions.explanation: Ground effect reduces induced drag, allowing the same lift at a lower angle of attack.

questions.question: By changing the angle of attack of a wing, the pilot can control the aeroplane's:
options: Lift and airspeed, but not drag.
Lift and drag, but not airspeed.
questions.explanation: Changing angle of attack changes lift and drag, which in turn affects airspeed.

questions.question: Which flight conditions of a large jet aeroplane create the most severe flight hazard by generating wingtip vortices of the greatest strength:
options: Heavy, slow, gear and flaps up.
Heavy, fast, gear and flaps down.
Heavy, slow, gear and flaps down.
Weight, gear and flaps make no difference.
questions.explanation: Wingtip vortices are strongest when the aircraft is heavy, slow, and clean.

questions.question: Hazardous vortex turbulence that might be encountered behind large aircraft is created only when that aircraft is:
questions.explanation: Wake vortices are produced whenever a wing is generating lift.

questions.question: Wingtip vortices created by large aircraft tend to:
options: Rise from the surface to traffic pattern altitude.
Sink below the aircraft generating the turbulence.
Accumulate and remain for a period of time at the point where the takeoff roll began.
Dissipate very slowly when the surface wind is strong.
questions.explanation: Wingtip vortices descend below the generating aircraft and drift with the wind.

questions.question: How does the wake turbulence vortex circulate around each wingtip, when viewed from the rear:
options: Inward, upward, and around the wingtip.
Outward, upward, and around the wingtip.
Outward, downward and around the wingtip.
questions.explanation: Wake vortices rotate outward, upward, and around each wingtip.

questions.question: Which statement is true concerning the wake turbulence produced by a large transport aircraft:
options: Wake turbulence behind a propeller-driven aircraft is negligible because jet engine thrust is a necessary factor.
Vortices can be avoided by flying 300 feet below and behind the generating aircraft.
The vortex characteristics of an aircraft may be altered by extending flaps or changing speed.
Vortices can be avoided by flying downwind of and below the generating aircraft.
questions.explanation: Flap configuration and speed influence vortex strength.

questions.question: What effect would a light crosswind have on the wingtip vortices generated by a large aeroplane that has just taken off:
options: The downwind vortex will remain on the runway longer.
A crosswind will rapidly dissipate both vortices.
A crosswind will move both vortices clear of the runway.
The upwind vortex will tend to remain on the runway longer than the downwind vortex.
questions.explanation: The downwind vortex drifts away while the upwind vortex remains closer to the runway.

questions.question: To avoid the wingtip vortices of a departing jet aeroplane during takeoff, the pilot should:
options: Climb above and stay upwind of the jet aeroplane's flightpath.
Lift off well past the jet aeroplane's flightpath.
Remain below and downwind of the jet aeroplane's flightpath.
questions.explanation: Stay above and upwind because vortices sink and drift with the wind.

questions.question: What wind condition prolongs the hazards of wake turbulence on a landing runway for the longest period of time:
questions.explanation: A light quartering tailwind can keep vortices over the runway longer.

questions.question: If you take off behind a heavy jet that has landed, you should plan to lift off:
options: Prior to the point where the jet touched down.
At the point where the jet touched down and on the upwind edge of the runway.
Before the point where the jet touched down and on the downwind edge of the runway.
Beyond the point where the jet touched down.
questions.explanation: Lift off beyond the touchdown point to avoid the descending wake vortices.

questions.question: The adverse effects of ice, snow, or frost on aircraft performance and flight characteristics include decreased lift and:
options: An aircraft will always stall at the same indicated airspeed.
questions.explanation: Ice, snow, or frost disrupts smooth airflow over the wing, reducing lift and increasing the stall speed.

questions.question: Lift on a wing is most properly defined as the:
options: Differential pressure acting perpendicular to the chord of the wing.
Force acting perpendicular to the relative wind.
Reduced pressure resulting from laminar flow over the upper camber of an aerofoil, acting perpendicular to the mean camber.
Force acting parallel with the relative wind and in the opposite direction.
questions.explanation: Lift is the aerodynamic force acting perpendicular to the relative airflow.

questions.question: Which statement is true relative to changing angle of attack:
options: A decrease in angle of attack will increase pressure below the wing and decrease drag.
An increase in angle of attack will decrease pressure below the wing and increase drag.
An increase in angle of attack will increase drag.
An increase in angle of attack will decrease the lift coefficient.
questions.explanation: Increasing angle of attack increases both lift and drag until the critical angle is reached.

questions.question: The angle of attack of a wing directly controls the:
options: Angle of incidence of the wing.
Distribution of pressures acting on the wing.
Amount of airflow above and below the wing.
Dynamic pressure acting in the airflow.
questions.explanation: Angle of attack changes the pressure distribution over the wing, thereby changing lift.

questions.question: In theory, if the angle of attack and other factors remain constant and the airspeed is doubled, the lift produced at the higher speed will be:
options: The same as at the lower speed.
Two times greater than at the lower speed.
Four times greater than at the lower speed.
questions.explanation: Lift is proportional to the square of airspeed. Doubling airspeed increases lift by four times.

questions.question: An aircraft wing is designed to produce lift resulting from a difference in the:
options: Negative air pressure below and a vacuum above the wing's surface.
Vacuum below the wing's surface and greater air pressure above the wing's surface.
Higher air pressure below the wing's surface and lower air pressure above the wing's surface.
Higher pressure at the leading edge than at the trailing edge.
questions.explanation: Lift is produced by higher pressure beneath the wing and lower pressure above it.

questions.question: On a wing, the force of lift acts perpendicular to, and the force of drag acts parallel to the:
questions.explanation: Lift acts perpendicular to the relative airflow (flightpath), while drag acts parallel to it.

questions.question: Which statement is true regarding the opposing forces acting on an aeroplane in steady-state level flight:
options: Thrust is greater than drag and weight and lift are equal.
Thrust is greater than drag and lift is greater than weight.
Thrust is slightly greater than lift, but drag and weight are equal.
questions.explanation: In steady, unaccelerated level flight, lift equals weight and thrust equals drag.

questions.question: At higher elevation airports the pilot should know that indicated airspeed:
options: Will be unchanged, but ground speed will be faster.
Will be higher, but ground speed will be unchanged.
Should be increased to compensate for the thinner air.
Should be higher to obtain a higher landing speed.
questions.explanation: IAS remains the same for the required lift, but TAS and ground speed are higher due to reduced air density.

questions.question: An aeroplane leaving ground effect will:
options: Experience a reduction in ground friction and require a slight power reduction.
Require a lower angle of attack to maintain the same lift coefficient.
Experience a reduction in induced drag and require a smaller angle of attack.
Experience an increase in induced drag and require more thrust.
questions.explanation: Leaving ground effect increases induced drag, requiring additional thrust to maintain performance.

questions.question: If the same angle of attack is maintained in ground effect as when out of ground effect, lift will:
options: Increase, and induced drag will decrease.
Increase, and induced drag will decrease.
Decrease, and induced drag will increase.
Decrease, and induced drag will decrease.
questions.explanation: Ground effect reduces induced drag, making the wing more efficient and increasing lift.

questions.question: Which is true regarding the force of lift in steady, unaccelerated flight:
options: There is a corresponding indicated airspeed required for every angle of attack to generate sufficient lift to maintain altitude.
An aerofoil will always stall at the same indicated airspeed; therefore, an increase in weight will require an increase in speed.
At lower airspeeds the angle of attack must be less to generate sufficient lift.
The lift force must be exactly equal to the drag force.
questions.explanation: Every angle of attack corresponds to a specific IAS required to produce the lift needed for level flight.

questions.question: At a given Indicated Air Speed, what effect will an increase in air density have on lift and drag:
options: Lift will increase but drag will decrease.
Lift and drag will remain the same.
questions.explanation: At a given IAS, the dynamic pressure is unchanged, so lift and drag remain the same.

questions.question: If the angle of attack is increased beyond the critical angle of attack, the wing will no longer produce sufficient lift to support the weight of the aircraft:
options: Unless the airspeed is greater than the normal stall speed.
Regardless of airspeed or pitch attitude.
Unless the pitch attitude is on or below the natural horizon.
In which case, the control column should be pulled back immediately.
questions.explanation: Exceeding the critical angle of attack causes an aerodynamic stall regardless of airspeed.

questions.question: Given that Aircraft A has a wingspan of 51 m and average wing chord of 4 m, and Aircraft B has a wingspan of 48 m and average wing chord of 3.5 m, determine the correct aspect ratio and wing area:
options: Aircraft A has an aspect ratio of 13.7 and has a larger wing area than Aircraft B.
Aircraft B has an aspect ratio of 13.7 and has a smaller wing area than Aircraft A.
Aircraft B has an aspect ratio of 12.75 and has a smaller wing area than Aircraft A.
Aircraft A has an aspect ratio of 12.75 and has a smaller wing area than Aircraft B.
questions.explanation: Aircraft B has the higher aspect ratio (≈13.7), while Aircraft A has the larger wing area.

questions.question: Aspect ratio of the wing is defined as the ratio of the:
options: Square of the chord to the wing span.
Wing span to the average chord.
Square of the wing area to the span.
questions.explanation: Aspect ratio is the wing span divided by the average chord.

questions.question: What changes to aircraft control must be made to maintain altitude while the airspeed is being decreased:
options: Increase the angle of attack to compensate for the decreasing dynamic pressure.
Maintain a constant angle of attack until the desired airspeed is reached, then increase the angle of attack.
Increase angle of attack to produce more lift than weight.
Decrease the angle of attack to compensate for the decrease in drag.
questions.explanation: As airspeed decreases, angle of attack must increase to maintain the required lift.

questions.question: Take-off from an airfield with a low density altitude will result in:
options: A higher than standard IAS before lift off.
A higher TAS for the same lift off IAS.
A shorter take-off run because of the lower TAS required for the same IAS.
questions.explanation: Low density altitude provides denser air, improving aircraft performance and reducing the take-off distance.

questions.question: What is the effect on total drag of an aircraft if the airspeed decreases in level flight below that speed for maximum L/D?
options: Drag increases because of increased induced drag.
Drag decreases because of lower induced drag.
Drag increases because of increased parasite drag.
Drag decreases because of lower parasite drag.
questions.explanation: Below the speed for maximum L/D, induced drag increases rapidly and causes total drag to increase.

questions.question: By changing the angle of attack of a wing, the pilot can control the airplane's:
options: Lift and airspeed, but not drag.
Lift and drag, but not airspeed.
questions.explanation: Changing angle of attack affects lift and drag, which in turn influences airspeed.

questions.question: What is the relationship between induced and parasite drag when the gross weight is increased?
options: Parasite drag increases more than induced drag.
Induced drag increases more than parasite drag.
Both parasite and induced drag are equally increased.
Both parasite and induced drag are equally decreased.
questions.explanation: A heavier aircraft requires more lift, increasing angle of attack and induced drag more significantly.

questions.question: In theory, if the airspeed of an airplane is doubled while in level flight, parasite drag will become:
questions.explanation: Parasite drag varies directly with the square of airspeed.

questions.question: As airspeed decreases in level flight below that speed for maximum lift/drag ratio, total drag of an aeroplane:
options: Decreases because of lower parasite drag.
Increases because of increased parasite drag.
Increases because of increased induced drag.
Decreases because of lower induced drag.
questions.explanation: Induced drag increases rapidly below L/Dmax speed, causing total drag to rise.

questions.question: (Refer to annex 'A') At the airspeed represented by point B, in steady flight, the airplane will:
options: Be developing its maximum coefficient of lift.
Be developing its minimum coefficient of drag.
questions.explanation: Point B represents the speed for maximum lift-to-drag ratio.

questions.question: Which statement is true relative to changing angle of attack?
options: A decrease in angle of attack will increase pressure below the wing, and decrease drag.
An increase in angle of attack will decrease pressure below the wing, and increase drag.
An increase in angle of attack will increase drag.
A decrease in angle of attack will decrease pressure below the wing and increase drag.
questions.explanation: Increasing angle of attack increases both induced drag and lift until the critical angle.

questions.question: On a wing, the force of lift acts perpendicular to, and the force of drag acts parallel to the:
questions.explanation: Lift acts perpendicular to the relative airflow, while drag acts parallel to it.

questions.question: The portion of the aircraft's total drag created by the production of lift is called:
options: Induced drag, and is greatly affected by changes in airspeed.
Induced drag, and is not affected by changes in airspeed.
Parasite drag, and is greatly affected by changes in airspeed.
Parasite drag, which is inversely proportional to the square of the airspeed.
questions.explanation: Induced drag is a by-product of lift and decreases as airspeed increases.

questions.question: The best L/D ratio of an aircraft occurs when parasite drag is:
questions.explanation: Maximum aerodynamic efficiency occurs when parasite drag equals induced drag.

questions.question: An aircraft has an L/D ratio of 15:1 at 50 knots in calm air. What would the L/D ratio be with a direct headwind of 25 knots?
questions.explanation: Lift-to-drag ratio depends on aircraft aerodynamics and is unaffected by wind.

questions.question: Which is true regarding aerodynamic drag?
options: Induced drag is a by-product of lift and is greatly affected by changes in airspeed.
All aerodynamic drag is created entirely by the production of lift.
Induced drag is created entirely by air resistance.
Parasite drag is a by-product of lift.
questions.explanation: Induced drag exists only because the wing is producing lift.

questions.question: At a given True Air Speed, what effect will increased air density have on the lift and drag of an aircraft?
options: Lift will increase but drag will decrease.
Lift and drag will remain the same.
questions.explanation: Greater air density increases both lift and drag for the same true airspeed.

questions.question: If the Indicated Air Speed of an aircraft is increased from 50 knots to 100 knots, parasite drag will be:
questions.explanation: Parasite drag increases with the square of airspeed.

questions.question: If the Indicated Air Speed of an aircraft is decreased from 100 knots to 50 knots, induced drag will be:
questions.explanation: Halving airspeed increases induced drag by approximately four times.

questions.question: The best L/D ratio of an aircraft in a given configuration is a value that:
options: Varies depending upon the weight being carried.
Remains constant regardless of Indicated Air Speed changes.
questions.explanation: The maximum lift-to-drag ratio is a characteristic of the aircraft's aerodynamic design and configuration.

questions.question: The tendency of an aircraft to develop forces which restore it to its original condition, when disturbed from a condition of steady flight, is known as:
questions.explanation: Stability is the tendency of an aircraft to return to its original state after being disturbed.

questions.question: As Indicated Air Speed increases in level flight, the total drag of an aircraft becomes greater than the total drag produced at the maximum lift/drag speed because of the:
questions.explanation: Above the speed for maximum L/D, parasite drag increases rapidly and becomes the dominant component of total drag.

questions.question: The resistance, or skin friction, due to the viscosity of the air as it passes along the surface of a wing is a type of:
questions.explanation: Skin friction drag is a component of parasite drag caused by the viscosity of the air.

questions.question: Which relationship is correct when comparing drag and airspeed?
options: Parasite drag varies inversely as the square of the airspeed.
Induced drag increases as the square of the airspeed.
Parasite drag increases as the square of the lift coefficient divided by the aspect ratio.
Induced drag varies inversely as the square of the airspeed.
questions.explanation: Induced drag decreases with increasing airspeed and is inversely proportional to the square of the airspeed.

questions.question: If the same angle of attack is maintained in ground effect as when out of ground effect, lift will:
options: Decrease, and parasite drag will decrease.
Increase, and induced drag will decrease.
Decrease, and parasite drag will increase.
Increase, and induced drag will increase.
questions.explanation: Ground effect reduces induced drag and increases lift for the same angle of attack.

questions.question: Which statement is true regarding aeroplane flight at L/Dmax?
options: Any angle of attack other than that for L/Dmax increases parasite drag.
Any angle of attack other than that for L/Dmax increases the lift/drag ratio.
Any angle of attack other than that for L/Dmax increases total drag for a given aeroplane's lift.
Any angle of attack other than that for L/Dmax increases lift and reduces drag.
questions.explanation: At L/Dmax the aircraft achieves minimum total drag. Any other angle of attack increases total drag for the same lift.

questions.question: Aspect ratio of a wing is defined as the ratio of the:
options: Square of the chord to the wingspan.
questions.explanation: Aspect ratio is the ratio of the wingspan to the mean aerodynamic chord.

questions.question: A wing with a very high aspect ratio (in comparison with a low aspect ratio wing) will have:
options: Poor control qualities at low airspeeds.
Increased drag at high angles of attack.
Reduced bending moment on its attachment points.
questions.explanation: According to the source, a high aspect ratio wing has poorer control qualities at low airspeeds.

questions.question: At a constant velocity in airflow, a high aspect ratio wing will have (in comparison with a low aspect ratio wing):
options: Increased drag, especially at a low angle of attack.
Decreased drag, especially at a high angle of attack.
Increased drag, especially at a high angle of attack.
Decreased drag, especially at low angles of attack.
questions.explanation: A high aspect ratio wing reduces induced drag, particularly at higher angles of attack.

questions.question: (Refer to Annex 'B') Which aircraft has the highest aspect ratio?
questions.explanation: According to the source, Aircraft A has the highest aspect ratio. (Requires Annex 'B' for reference.)

questions.question: (Refer to Annex 'B') Which aircraft has the lowest aspect ratio?
questions.explanation: According to the source, Aircraft B has the lowest aspect ratio. (Requires Annex 'B' for reference.)

questions.question: (Refer to Annex 'B') Consider only aspect ratio (other factors remain constant). Which aircraft will generate greatest lift?
questions.explanation: According to the source, Aircraft B generates the greatest lift when considering aspect ratio alone. (Requires Annex 'B' for reference.)

questions.question: (Refer to Annex 'B') Consider only aspect ratio (other factors remain constant). Which aircraft will generate greatest drag?
questions.explanation: According to the source, Aircraft A generates the greatest drag when considering aspect ratio alone. (Requires Annex 'B' for reference.)

questions.question: What happens to total drag when accelerating from CLMAX to maximum speed?
questions.explanation: According to the source, total drag increases as the aircraft accelerates from CLMAX to maximum speed.

questions.question: (Refer to Annex 'C'). The whole aircraft CL against CD polar. Point 'B' represents:
questions.explanation: According to the source, Point B represents the critical angle of attack. (Requires Annex 'C' for reference.)

questions.question: If the Indicated Air Speed of an aircraft in level flight is increased from 100 kt to 200 kt, what change will occur in (i) TAS (ii) CDi (iii) Di?
questions.explanation: According to the source, doubling IAS doubles TAS, reduces the coefficient of induced drag to one-sixteenth, and reduces induced drag to one-quarter.

questions.question: An aeroplane will stall at the same:
options: Angle of attack and attitude with relation to the horizon
Airspeed regardless of the attitude with relation to the horizon
Angle of attack regardless of the attitude with relation to the horizon
Indicated airspeed regardless of altitude, bank angle and load factor
questions.explanation: A wing always stalls at the same critical angle of attack, which is a fixed aerodynamic property of the aerofoil section. Attitude, airspeed, altitude, bank angle and load factor can all vary at the point of stall, but the angle of attack at which the airflow separates does not change.

questions.question: A typical stalling angle of attack for a wing without sweepback is:
questions.explanation: For a conventional unswept wing, the critical (stalling) angle of attack is typically around 15°–16°. Beyond this angle the airflow separates from the upper surface faster than lift can be generated, causing a sharp loss of lift.

questions.question: If the aircraft weight is increased without change of C of G position, the stalling angle of attack will:
options: The position of the CG does not affect the stall speed
questions.explanation: The stalling angle of attack is a fixed characteristic of the wing's aerofoil section and is independent of weight. Increasing weight increases the stalling speed (since more lift, and therefore more dynamic pressure, is needed to reach maximum lift coefficient), but the angle of attack at which the stall occurs is unchanged.

questions.question: If the angle of attack is increased above the stalling angle:
options: Lift and drag will both decrease
Lift will decrease and drag will increase
Lift will increase and drag will decrease
Lift and drag will both increase
questions.explanation: Beyond the critical angle of attack, the airflow separates from the upper surface of the wing. This separation causes the lift coefficient to fall away rapidly while the drag coefficient continues to rise steeply due to the large area of turbulent, separated flow.

questions.question: The angle of attack at which an aeroplane stalls:
options: Will occur at smaller angles of attack flying downwind than when flying upwind
Is dependent upon the speed of the airflow over the wing
Is a function of speed and density altitude
Will remain constant regardless of gross weight
questions.explanation: The stalling angle of attack is fixed by the aerofoil's geometry and surface condition, not by weight, speed, altitude, or wind direction relative to the ground. Groundspeed and wind have no bearing on angle of attack, since angle of attack depends only on the relationship between the wing chord and the relative airflow.

questions.question: An aircraft whose weight is 237,402 N stalls at 132 kt. At a weight of 356,103 N it would stall at:
questions.explanation: Stalling speed varies with the square root of the weight ratio: Vs2 = Vs1 × √(W2/W1). Here, W2/W1 = 356,103 / 237,402 = 1.5, and √1.5 ≈ 1.2247. So Vs2 = 132 × 1.2247 ≈ 162 kt.

questions.question: For an aircraft with a 1 g stalling speed of 60 kt IAS, the stalling speed in a steady 60° turn would be:
questions.explanation: In a steady, level turn, the load factor n = 1 / cos(bank angle). At 60° bank, n = 1 / cos60° = 1 / 0.5 = 2. Stalling speed increases with the square root of the load factor: Vs(turn) = Vs(1g) × √n = 60 × √2 ≈ 84.8 kt, rounded to 84 kt.

questions.question: For an aircraft in a steady turn the stalling speed would be:
options: The same as in level flight
At a lower speed than in level flight
At a higher speed than in level flight, and a lower angle of attack
At a higher speed than in level flight and at the same angle of attack
questions.explanation: A stall always occurs at the same critical angle of attack regardless of the flight condition. In a turn, the increased load factor means more lift (and therefore a higher airspeed at the same angle of attack) is required to balance the increased apparent weight, so the stalling speed rises while the stalling angle of attack stays the same.

questions.question: Formation of ice on the wing leading edge will:
options: Cause the aircraft to stall at a higher speed and a higher angle of attack
Cause the aircraft to stall at a higher speed and a lower angle of attack
Cause the aircraft to stall at a lower speed
questions.explanation: Ice accretion on the leading edge disrupts the smooth airflow over the wing, causing the airflow to separate earlier. This reduces the maximum lift coefficient (CLmax) the wing can achieve, so the wing reaches its maximum lift capability, and therefore stalls, at a lower angle of attack but a higher airspeed than it would when clean.

questions.question: Dividing lift by weight gives:
questions.explanation: Load factor (n) is defined as the ratio of the lift produced by the wings to the total weight of the aircraft (n = L/W). In straight and level, unaccelerated flight, load factor equals 1, since lift exactly balances weight.

questions.question: The stalling speed of an aeroplane is most affected by:
questions.explanation: Stalling speed (IAS) is most directly and significantly affected by changes in the aircraft's weight, or "loading" (fuel, passengers, cargo, or load factor in a turn). While air density affects true airspeed at the stall, indicated stalling speed for a given configuration and load factor stays essentially constant with altitude.

questions.question: Stalling may be delayed to a higher angle of attack by:
options: Increasing the surface roughness of the wing top surface
Distortion of the leading edge by ice build-up
Increasing the kinetic energy of the boundary layer
questions.explanation: The stall occurs when the boundary layer no longer has enough kinetic energy to overcome the adverse pressure gradient on the upper surface, causing separation. Increasing the boundary layer's kinetic energy, for example through slots, slats, or boundary layer control, allows the airflow to remain attached to a higher angle of attack before separating.

questions.question: A stall inducer strip will:
options: Cause the wing to stall first at the root
Cause the wing to stall at the tip first
Re-energise the boundary layer at the wing root
questions.explanation: Stall inducer (stall) strips are small triangular fittings attached to the leading edge near the wing root. They deliberately disturb and thicken the boundary layer at the root at high angles of attack, causing that area to stall first. This is a safety feature: with the root stalling before the tip, the ailerons near the tip remain effective for longer, preserving roll control as the stall develops.

questions.question: On a highly tapered wing without wing twist the stall will commence:
options: At the centre of the span
questions.explanation: On a wing with strong taper (tip chord much smaller than root chord) and no washout, the local lift coefficient is higher toward the tip than at the root for a given overall angle of attack. Since the tip reaches its local CLmax first, the stall begins at the tip, which is undesirable as it can reduce aileron effectiveness and stall warning quality.

questions.question: Sweepback on a wing will:
options: Reduce induced drag at low speed
Increase the tendency to tip stall
Reduce the tendency to tip stall
Cause the stall to occur at a lower angle of attack
questions.explanation: On a swept wing, spanwise (outward) airflow develops along the wing due to the sweep angle, causing the boundary layer to thicken progressively toward the tip. This makes the tip region prone to earlier separation, increasing the tendency for the wing to stall at the tips first.

questions.question: The purpose of a boundary layer fence on a swept wing is:
options: To re-energise the boundary layer and prevent separation
To control spanwise flow and delay tip stall
To generate a vortex over the upper surface of the wing
To maintain a laminar boundary layer
questions.explanation: A boundary layer fence is a flat plate mounted chordwise on the upper surface of a swept wing. It acts as a barrier to the spanwise flow of the boundary layer toward the tip, keeping the boundary layer thinner and healthier outboard, which delays the onset of tip stall.

questions.question: A wing with washout would have:
options: The tip chord less than the root chord
The tip incidence less than the root incidence
The tip incidence greater than the root incidence
The tip camber less than the root camber
questions.explanation: Washout is a form of geometric wing twist in which the angle of incidence progressively decreases from root to tip. This means the tip is set at a lower angle of attack than the root, so as the overall angle of attack increases, the root reaches its critical angle of attack, and stalls, before the tip does.

questions.question: On an untapered wing without twist the downwash:
options: Is greatest at centre span, less at root and tip
questions.explanation: Because of the trailing (wingtip) vortices generated at the tips, the induced downwash increases progressively from the root out toward the tip on a straight, untwisted wing, reducing the effective angle of attack more toward the tips than at the root.

questions.question: A wing of constant thickness which is not swept back:
options: Will stall at the tip first due to the increase in spanwise flow
Could drop a wing at the stall due to the lack of any particular stall inducing characteristics
Will pitch nose down approaching the stall due to the forward movement of the centre of pressure
Will stall evenly across the span
questions.explanation: A rectangular, unswept, untwisted wing has no built-in feature (such as washout, a stall strip, or sweep-induced spanwise flow) to control precisely where the stall begins. Small manufacturing variations, turbulence, or asymmetric control inputs can therefore cause one wing to stall slightly before the other, resulting in an unpredictable wing drop at the stall.

questions.question: Slots increase the stalling angle of attack by:
options: Reducing the effective angle of attack
questions.explanation: A slot allows high-energy air from below the wing to accelerate through a gap near the leading edge and flow over the upper surface. This re-energises the boundary layer, giving it more kinetic energy to resist the adverse pressure gradient, which delays airflow separation and allows the wing to reach a higher angle of attack before stalling.

questions.question: A rectangular wing, when compared to other wing planforms, has a tendency to stall first at the:
options: Wing root, providing adequate stall warning
Leading edge, where the wing root joins the fuselage
questions.explanation: A rectangular (untapered) wing has a lift distribution that is highest toward the root, so the root reaches its critical angle of attack first. This is beneficial because the disturbed, separated airflow from the root can buffet the tailplane and fuselage, giving the pilot natural pre-stall buffet warning, while the ailerons near the still-flying tips remain effective.

questions.question: Vortex generators are used:
options: To counteract the effect of the wing-tip vortices
questions.explanation: Vortex generators are small vane-like fins mounted on the wing's upper surface. They create small trailing vortices that mix high-energy air from outside the boundary layer into the slower-moving boundary layer, re-energising it and delaying flow separation, which improves control and lift characteristics at high angles of attack.

questions.question: A stick shaker is:
options: An overspeed warning device that operates at high Mach numbers
A device to vibrate the control column to give a stall warning
A device to prevent a stall by giving a pitch down
questions.explanation: A stick shaker is a mechanical device, usually an eccentric motor driving the control column, that vibrates the control yoke or stick to give the pilot a tactile (and audible) warning of an approaching stall, typically triggered by an angle of attack sensor, before the actual stall occurs.

questions.question: A stall warning device must be set to operate:
options: At a speed just below the stalling speed
At a speed about 5% to 10% above the stalling speed
At a speed about 20% above the stalling speed
questions.explanation: Certification requirements specify that a stall warning must occur with sufficient margin before the actual stall, typically at a speed roughly 5–10% above the stalling speed (or an equivalent margin in angle of attack), giving the pilot adequate time to react before the wing actually stalls.

questions.question: Just before the stall the wing leading edge stagnation point is positioned:
options: On top of the stall warning vane
On top of the leading edge because of the extremely high angle of attack
questions.explanation: As angle of attack increases toward the stall, the stagnation point (where the oncoming airflow divides to pass over and under the wing) moves down and aft along the underside of the leading edge. This causes airflow to be deflected upward past the stall warning vane, which is mounted so as to detect this shift and trigger the warning.

questions.question: A wing mounted stall warning detector vane would be situated:
options: On the upper surface at about mid chord
On the lower surface at about mid chord
At the leading edge on the lower surface
At the leading edge on the upper surface
questions.explanation: The stall warning vane is mounted at the leading edge, on the lower surface, at the point where the stagnation point sits during normal cruise flight. As the angle of attack increases and the stagnation point moves aft and below the vane, airflow is deflected upward over the vane, which mechanically or electrically triggers the stall warning.

questions.question: The input data to a stall warning device (e.g. stick shaker) system is:
options: Angle of attack, and in some systems rate of change of angle of attack
Airspeed and sometimes rate of change of airspeed
questions.explanation: Modern stall warning and stick shaker systems are primarily driven by angle of attack sensors, since the stall itself is fundamentally an angle of attack phenomenon rather than an airspeed one. Some systems also factor in the rate of change of angle of attack to anticipate a rapidly developing stall, such as during abrupt manoeuvring.

questions.question: A stick pusher is:
options: A device to prevent an aircraft from stalling
A device to assist the pilot to move the controls at high speed
A device which automatically compensates for pitch changes at high speed
questions.explanation: A stick pusher is a flight control device that automatically pushes the control column forward when a stall is imminent, forcibly reducing the angle of attack. It is a more forceful safeguard than a stick shaker, actively preventing the aircraft from reaching the critical angle of attack, and is often fitted to aircraft with poor natural stall warning characteristics.

questions.question: In a developed spin:
options: The angle of attack of both wings will be positive
The angle of attack of both wings will be negative
The angle of attack of one wing will be positive and the other will be negative
The down going wing will be stalled and the up going wing will not be stalled
questions.explanation: In a fully developed spin, both wings are stalled and both are at a positive angle of attack beyond the critical angle. The down-going (inner) wing is at a higher angle of attack than the up-going (outer) wing due to its additional downward rotational velocity, producing an autorotative rolling moment, but both wings remain stalled throughout.

questions.question: To recover from a spin, the elevators should be:
options: Moved up to increase the angle of attack
Moved down to reduce the angle of attack
questions.explanation: Since a spin is fundamentally a stalled condition on both wings, recovery requires reducing the angle of attack below the critical angle. Moving the elevator (control column) forward achieves this, allowing the airflow to reattach to the wings so that normal lift and control effectiveness can be restored.

questions.question: High speed buffet (shock stall) is caused by:
options: The boundary layer separating in front of a shockwave at high angles of attack
The boundary layer separating immediately behind the shock wave
The shock wave striking the tail of the aircraft
The shock wave striking the fuselage
questions.explanation: At high subsonic/transonic speeds, a shockwave can form on the wing's upper surface where local airflow becomes supersonic. The sudden pressure rise across this shockwave causes the boundary layer immediately behind it to separate from the surface, producing buffet and a loss of lift known as the high-speed or shock stall.

questions.question: In a 30° bank level turn, the stall speed will be increased by:
questions.explanation: In a level turn, load factor n = 1 / cos(bank angle). At 30° bank, n = 1 / cos30° = 1 / 0.866 = 1.1547. The increase in stalling speed is proportional to √n = √1.1547 ≈ 1.0746, which is an increase of approximately 7% over the 1g stalling speed.

questions.question: Heavy rain can increase the stall speed of an aircraft for which of the following reasons?
options: Water increases the viscosity of air
Heavy rain can block the pitot tube, giving false airspeed indications
The extra weight and distortion of the aerodynamic surfaces by the film of water
The impact of heavy rain will slow the aircraft
questions.explanation: A film of water adhering to the wing surface in heavy rain disrupts the smooth airflow (effectively acting similarly to roughness or light contamination) and adds a small amount of extra weight, both of which reduce the maximum lift coefficient achievable and therefore increase the stalling speed.

questions.question: If the tailplane is supplying a download and stalls due to contamination by ice:
options: The wing will stall and the aircraft will pitch-up due to the weight of the ice behind the aircraft CG
The increased weight on the tailplane due to the ice formation will pitch the aircraft nose up, which will stall the wing
Because it was supplying a download the aircraft will pitch nose up
The aircraft will pitch nose down
questions.explanation: A conventional tailplane normally produces a downward force (download) to balance the nose-down pitching moment of the wing. If ice contamination causes the tailplane to stall, this download is suddenly lost. The loss of the tailplane's downward force allows the nose to pitch down abruptly, which can be sudden and severe, especially when flaps are extended.

questions.question: Indications of an icing-induced stall can be: .1. An artificial stall warning device. .2. Airspeed close to the normal stall speed. .3. Violent roll oscillations. .4. Airframe buffet. .5. Violent wing drop. .6. Extremely high rate of descent while in a 'normal' flight attitude.
questions.explanation: An ice-contaminated tailplane or wing stall often occurs without conventional warning, since normal stall warning systems and airspeed margins may not reflect the degraded, contaminated aerofoil. Instead, the typical indications are violent roll oscillations, airframe buffet, sudden and violent wing drop, and an unusually high rate of descent while the aircraft still appears to be in a normal pitch attitude.

questions.question: If a light single engine propeller aircraft is stalled, power-on, in a climbing turn to the left, which of the following is the preferred recovery action?
options: Elevator stick forward, ailerons stick neutral, rudder to prevent wing drop
Elevator stick neutral, rudder neutral, ailerons to prevent wing drop, power to idle
Elevator stick forward, ailerons and rudder to prevent wing drop
Elevator stick neutral, rudder neutral, ailerons stick neutral, power to idle
questions.explanation: The standard stall recovery technique is to move the control column forward to reduce the angle of attack immediately, keep the ailerons neutral (since using ailerons near the stall can aggravate a wing drop into an incipient spin), and use rudder alone to prevent or correct any yaw/wing-drop tendency, while managing power as appropriate for the type.

questions.question: If the stick shaker activates on a swept wing jet transport aircraft immediately after take-off while turning, which of the following statements contains the preferred course of action?
options: Monitor the instruments to ensure it is not a spurious warning
questions.explanation: The stick shaker is a direct and immediate warning of an impending stall based on angle of attack. The correct and immediate response is to reduce the angle of attack, typically by easing forward pressure on the controls, to restore a safe margin above the stall, rather than delaying to verify the warning or relying solely on thrust or bank angle changes, which do not directly address the angle of attack problem.
